item.content:encoded:
Promotion: subtly reflective silver-grey glass and tactile physical controls characterise Fisher & Paykel's Contemporary Style kitchen appliances, designed with versatility for the social heart of the home.
The Contemporary appliances are one of three product design styles in the New Zealand company's luxury range, alongside the Minimal and Professional offerings.

Fisher & Paykel explained that each of its curated styles supports architects, designers and homeowners in creating bespoke kitchens with a cohesive aesthetic.

"The advantage is a consistent design language across the appliance collection, from cooking and cooling to wine care and dishwashing," said the brand.

Fisher & Paykel's Contemporary Style includes flush-fitting ovens and cooktops as well as an expansive ecosystem of complementary appliances, all with the same focus on clean lines, softly silver surfaces and comfortable interaction.

Its aesthetic contrasts with the Minimal Style, where dark colours and dial- and handle-free designs allow the products to recede into the background.

Together, the style families are intended to enable the creation of bespoke spaces befitting the evolving role of the domestic kitchen.
Fisher & Paykel explained that once hidden from view, kitchens are now one of the main social spaces in the home.

They attract a constant thrum of activity as families join in meal preparation, guests hover and chat, and daily rituals are tended to.

Within this context, the brand's style families bring the "beauty of choice" to architects, designers and homeowners in the luxury market, letting them pick products for both their function and cohesion with a material palette.

For the Contemporary range, Fisher & Paykel focused on a timeless appearance, with clean lines and tonal contrasts. Knowledge of interaction and how people experience the space was also taken into consideration.

The brushed silver glass on the ovens has an "active relationship with its surroundings", said the company, picking up on the tones of surrounding materials like stone and timber and gently shifting its appearance as the light changes throughout the day.

"The silver-grey glass finish was designed to create depth and subtle reflectivity within the kitchen," said Fisher & Paykel head of industrial design (cooking) Adam Moody.

"As light changes throughout the day, the products reveal different qualities and relationships with surrounding materials."

The Contemporary range is intended to complement both light and dark interiors, either adding contrast and depth through reflectivity
in darker spaces, or reading softly against pale cabinetry, tile and stone.

"With Contemporary Style, we wanted to create a refined material presence: expressive enough to add depth and character to the kitchen, but restrained enough to work across a wide range of architectural interiors," added Moody.

Fisher & Paykel marries these finishes with precisely machined dials, round bar handles that sit comfortably in the hand and carefully calibrated door movement, emphasising tactility.

This is complemented with intuitive touchscreens and SmartHQ app connectivity for detailed and remote control.

The Contemporary line includes steam, convection and combination ovens as well as companion products such as vacuum seal drawers and warming drawers.

Gas or induction hobs are also available, with stainless steel or black glass finishes. Refrigerators, wine cabinets, range cookers, cooker hoods and dishwashers complete the offering.

The Contemporary Style products are designed for flush-fit installation and sit precisely within cabinetry, with only fine gaps as small as two millimetres. There are 60- and 76-centimetre formats to suit different layouts.

Fisher & Paykel was founded in New Zealand in 1934. Find out more about the company and its Contemporary Style luxury appliances on its website.

item.content:encoded:
Canadian studio RHAD Architects has completed Two Bay House in Nova Scotia, Canada, which consists of blocky volumes with carved-out voids, mass-timber framing and blackened wood cladding.

The waterfront home is located within a family estate on Cape Breton Island, in northeastern Nova Scotia.

The design began with two simple masses, which were then strategically carved away to form courtyards, terraces and double-height spaces.  These voids were designed to "mediate between shelter and landscape".

"The architecture emerges not through the addition of elements, but through a series of deliberate acts of subtraction and carving," said RHAD Architects, a studio based in Dartmouth, Nova Scotia, and led by founder Rayleen Hill.

"The resulting voids are as significant as the forms themselves, becoming the spaces through which the house is experienced."

The house rises two levels and is partly made of mass timber. Its primary roof structure consists of glue-laminated timber, while the roof decking is standard lumber.

The walls are made of insulated concrete forms (ICFs).

In plan, it consists of two parallel bars, or "bays", with one shorter in length.

"Their differing lengths establish a protected, west-facing courtyard that shelters outdoor living from prevailing waterfront winds while capturing afternoon sunlight," the team said.

Exterior walls are clad in vertical wooden siding that was charred using shou sugi ban (yakisugi), an ancient Japanese technique. Treated with black oil, the burnt wood "gives the building a quiet, monolithic presence within the landscape".

In carved-away areas, the solid charred wood gives way to slatted wood and vertical-grain hemlock siding.

"The contrast between charred and natural wood makes each subtraction legible, revealing the spaces where the architecture opens itself to light, landscape and occupation," the team said.

The home is entered on the east, where one finds an entry court enclosed within tall, slatted walls.

Filtered sunlight passes into the threshold, creating changing patterns throughout the day, while the enclosure glows in the evening from internal light.

The vertical space acts as a "constant point of reference" within the home, the team said.

Inside, there is a division between communal and private areas.

The shorter of the two volumes contains two bedrooms on the bottom level and a primary bedroom up above.

The longer volume holds a kitchen, dining area and living room on the ground floor. Upstairs, there is a music room and a small salon, as one of the clients is a hairstylist.

A large portion of the upper floor is carved away, forming a void in the centre of the house. A loft and glass-walled bridge overlook the communal area, "allowing light, conversation and activity to move freely between levels".

Along the water-facing side of the house, ample glazing and covered terraces extend the interior living spaces outward – "allowing the architecture to project into the landscape while maintaining a strong sense of enclosure", the team said.

The west side of the house features a swimming pool surrounded by a generous terrace.

Overall, it was designed to show "how subtraction can generate richness," the studio said.

 

"Rather than relying on formal complexity, it demonstrates how carefully carved voids can produce moments of compression and release, darkness and light, intimacy and openness.

"The result is a home whose character is defined as much by the spaces removed as by those that remain."

Other homes in Nova Scotia include a cedar-wrapped house by Omar Gandhi Architects that sits on a rocky coastline, and a residence by MacKay-Lyons Sweetapple that is a "village" of gabled steel structures.

The photography is by Adrian Ozimek.

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studio HKS has unveiled interior designs for the upcoming Washington Commanders NFL stadium in Washington DC, showing what its glass ceiling will look like.

The renderings showcase a steep bowl underneath the glass ceiling, giving fans an idea of the much-anticipated 70,000-seat stadium ahead of its construction.

Noteworthy is the continuous ring of stands, designed without the interruption from protruding box seats or the overhangs typical of most NFL-sized stadiums.

HKS architect Aaron Hollis said that the priority was a unified viewing experience for fans.

"We designed this bowl from the inside out, starting with a single question: what should it feel like when every fan is part of the game?" said Hollis.

"Every decision, from the steepness of the seating to the elimination of overhangs, was driven by that question. The result is a single, unified bowl where nothing separates the fans from the action or from each other."

Digital banners are shown running around select tiers, with a large banner wrapping the top of the stadium. In some images, the digital banners are shown reflecting off the glass ceiling.

When the initial exterior renderings were announced, HKS emphasised its intention to design both deferentially and referentially to the architecture of the US capital.

Read:

Four upcoming NFL stadiums that show the future of the league

This principle seems to have continued on the inside – the stands open up at one end to directly frame the dome of the US Capitol building.

The design of the bowl was informed by RFK Stadium, which is being demolished to make way for the HKS design.

HKS also emphasised the loudness of the design and said the elements work together "to capture crowd noise inside the stadium and push it back down toward the field".

"The result: one of the loudest stadiums in the NFL," said the studio.

The stadium design has become a national talking point. Earlier this year, an aide to US president Donald Trump suggested the stadium should be "classical" in line with the administration's executive order giving precedent to the style across federal buildings.

The stadium's site near the Anacostia River is administered by local government and falls outside of the mandate. Still, the architecture studio integrated columns on the exterior that are modern in form but capture some elements of classical ornamentation.

The Washington Commanders Stadium at the RFK Campus is set to open around 2030.

The images are courtesy of the Washington Commanders.

item.content:encoded:
Austrian studio Lechner & Lechner Architects has added an annexe clad in charred timber to a house in the Alps, designed as a minimalist space to "withdraw and think".

Named Quiet Retreat, the pared-back annexe sits as a standalone multipurpose room alongside an existing home in Salzkammergut, Austria, creating a loosely U-shaped ensemble around a central patio.

Lechner & Lechner Architects designed the space to feel "open but never exposed", with a wall of foldable glass doors along one edge overlooking woodland, a rocky outcrop and expansive views across meadows and the Alps in the distance.

"The landscape was really the starting point of the project," studio partner Paul Lechner told Dezeen.

"The existing rock and the building form a kind of natural atrium on a small rise. From there, the space opens towards the meadows and the surrounding mountains," added Lechner.

"We wanted the house to feel open to the landscape, but never exposed. Finding that balance was something we worked on throughout the design process," he added.

Read:

Mossy rooftop crowns Bather's Cabin in East Sussex woodland

The space has been purposefully left free of any fitted elements that would suggest a specific purpose, save for a series of climbing holds on one of its walls and a traditional Alpine bell hung from the ceiling.

A single window at one end of the annexe frames views of the adjacent forest, while on the long edge of the space folding glass doors open the interior up to a gravel patio sheltered by the rocky outcrop.

"Rather than separating different activities into individual rooms, the space is used as a place for creative work, writing, playing and simply spending time there," Lechner said. "It is also a quiet place to withdraw and think."

Atop a slim concrete base, the dark, charred-timber cladding of Quiet Retreat was chosen as a nod to traditional black Alpine barns, and achieved using the Japanese technique of Shou Sugi Ban.

To create contrast in the interiors, the walls and gabled ceiling are entirely lined in pale panels of oriented strand board (OSB).

"The contrast between the dark exterior and the lighter interior became an important part of the character of the house," Lechner told Dezeen. "There is also a connection to Alpine building traditions, where timber facades naturally become darker, greyer and more weathered over time."

"By charring the timber, the building does not have this very new appearance at the beginning. It feels more settled in the landscape from day one," he added.

Other projects in the Austrian Alps recently featured on Dezeen include the renovation of a 17th-century Alpine lodge into a boutique hotel by owners and architects Gerold and Katia Schneider, and a shingle-clad viewing tower on a mountain peak by Snøhetta.

The photography is by Julian Höck.

item.content:encoded:
Artist Isamaya Ffrench has opened her second-ever Studio Iron show as part of this year's London Design Festival, with participants including Andu Masebo and Barnaby Lewis.

Studio Iron is the brainchild of Ffrench, a makeup artist and creative director, who launched her collectible design gallery at Saatchi Yates earlier this year.

The project is back for London Design Festival (LDF), on display as part of curator Alex Tieghi-Walker's Perfectly Imperfect programme in the Brompton Design District.

Ffrench selected 27 creatives for the exhibition, featuring pieces that challenge ideas about what materials go together.

"Our designers are based all over the world, and as someone who's highly into the tactility of objects and art, it was amazing to see all the pieces in real life," she told Dezeen. "To see how they looked, what they felt like, and to witness their scale."

"Most of the time, we get to experience art and design on the internet, in museums or in shops as the finished piece with great lighting and great props," she continued.

"But I'm more interested in the process, the tools, the raw materials, and the industrial machines. It's a real privilege to be in an artist's space and to talk to them about their inspiration or see them at work."

Among the selection is a low-slung hammered steel pouf by Jesse Butterfield, topped with a lacy linen cushion by Jane Wright.

Opposite the pouf, an oversized, angular armchair by tattoo artist Thomas Cardiff is on display, crafted from a steel frame with a cowhide-clad seat and tattooed leather sides.

Marten Herma Anderson is showing a bloated resin lamp with a gridded pattern and a nickel-plated brass base, while Atelier Fomenta is presenting a bulb encased in a cylindrical slab of rubber held together with rivets.

A tangled stainless steel coat rack by Andu Masebo was placed in the corner of the gallery, close to a chunky hammered steel mirror, also by Butterfield.

Blacksmith Barnaby Lewis's spindly, skeletal chair features in the show, alongside a stainless steel floor lamp by Wretched Flowers, cloaked in chainmail, gemstones and glass beads.

Lewis is among the London-based rising talents spotlighted in the Dezeen Dispatch newspaper we published for LDF.

"Barnaby's practice is visceral and poetic at the same time and he's also wildly prolific," Ffrench told Dezeen. "His work deserves more attention."

Read:

London has "the best architecture and interior design community in Europe" says Duncan Riches

London-based Ffrench said that she hopes to expand Studio Iron, which is still in its infancy, into an interdisciplinary creative agency that champions young designers.

"London feels genuinely open in terms of how people work," said the artist. "There's less pressure to attach yourself to a single practice, which makes it easier to move between disciplines."

"Galleries and shops are also much more inclined to represent and sell the work of emerging artists versus established ones," added Ffrench. "And I think it is vital to support them and help them grow."

LDF is in full swing in the UK capital, with current shows ranging from a lighting installation by Lee Broom to the launch of prototype furniture and object platform Lobby.

The photography is by Andy Stagg.

The Studio Iron show is on show from 12 to 20 September as part of London Design Festival. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

item.content:encoded:
Dezeen Showroom: 1970s-style curves meet creative textural contrast in the Nina lounge chair, designed by Patricia Urquiola for furniture brand Andreu World.

The Nina lounge chair has a bulbous, organic shape that looks almost pebble-like from the front, which flows in a continuous, looping curve around itself, forming a sculptural back.

Andreu World says the shape was inspired by the 1656 Diego Velázquez painting Las Meninas, where the subjects wear oversized, enveloping crinolines, as well as paying homage to the "expressive freedom" of 1970s furniture.

Instead of being entirely upholstered, the chair features gentle juxtaposition from a hard structural back shell made of the Spanish brand's Pure ECO thermopolymer, produced from 100 per cent recycled polymer waste.

This shell is available in a glossy or matt enamel finish and features a pockmarked organic relief reminiscent of stone. Inspired by surfaces shaped by water, it brings extra personality to the already commanding chair.

Made from high-quality technical foams and carefully tailored upholstery, Patricia Urquiola intended for the Nina lounge chair to be used in both residential and professional environments, where its wide, armless seat invites easy repose.

item.content:encoded:
A land reclamation project has added the equivalent of 42 football pitches to Denmark's southern coast, as part of the construction of the Fehmarnbelt Tunnel under the Baltic Sea.

Fehmarnbelt Tunnel is an 18-kilometre-long road-and-rail tunnel, set to be the longest of its kind in the world. It is being built to connect Denmark and Germany and improve links between continental Europe and Scandinavia.

Seabed excavations from the project have been repurposed as an artificial island measuring approximately 300,000 square metres on the coast of Rødbyhavn, which is set to be landscaped as a nature spot.

"People can experience distinctive coastal nature"

State-owned transport company Sund & Bælt, which is developing the project, said the land will "become a unique experience for visitors".

“We have reused material from the seabed to create an area where people can experience distinctive coastal nature, with walking trails, ponds and wildlife including birds, amphibians and insects," said project manager Ditte Hjort.

"What makes the new area so special is that visitors can follow nature’s development right from the outset. We hope it will become a unique experience for visitors, with salt marshes and rich, diverse wildlife and plant life."

The 18-kilometre tunnel is being built to connect Rødbyhavn in Denmark with Puttgarden in Germany, and is scheduled for completion in 2029.

It will be formed of 89 concrete elements,, measuring 217 metres in length and 73,000 tonnes in weight, which will be submerged and combined in a man-made trench in the seabed.

It is expected to reduce journey times between Hamburg and Copenhagen to two hours by train and just over an hour by road, minimising dependence on flying.

Native plants will cover the land

The 300,000 square metres of land that has been added to Denmark as part of the project is set to be landscaped with three ponds and planting to withstand harsh coastal climate.

Soil that was excavated to build a factory from the tunnel has also been spread across the site, containing plant seeds that are hoped to bring life to the new landscape.

Read:

Artificial island Lynetteholm to be built in Copenhagen harbour

An agreement between Denmark and Germany to build the tunnel was signed in 2008, but delays followed due to opposition from ferry operators and conservation groups.

Elsewhere in Denmark, an artificial island called Lynetteholm is currently under development off the coast of Copenhagen to house 35,000 people and act as a defence against rising sea levels.

Architecture studio Urban Power is also designing nine artificial islands, named Holmene, off the coast of the city that will become a sustainable tech hub.

item.content:encoded:
A Matti Suuronen Futuro House has been manufactured for the first time in decades and decked out by Finnish design brand Marimekko for Helsinki Design Week.

The famously flying-saucer-like structure recently landed in Kaisaniemi Botanical Gardens as part of the Finnish capital's annual design festival.

Initially conceived as a transportable ski cabin by Finnish architect Matti Suuronen in 1968, the Futuro House is among the most distinctive emblems of space-age architecture.

Prefrabricated in fibreglass-reinforced plastic, it was once described by British critic Justin McGuirk as "the closest housing ever came to product design".

Despite being intended for mass production, fewer than 100 were made worldwide. Manufacture ceased shortly after the 1973 oil crisis, which sent the price of plastic rocketing.

Around 60 are estimated to still be in existence, scattered across the globe in varying states of repair.

That number became one greater recently for the first time in decades, thanks to a project that began in 2024 when Dutch-American preservationist architect Jan van Dijs was alerted by a friend and client to an unusual post on Facebook.

An executive at a Finnish materials firm, Exel Composites, was selling the original Futuro moulds.

"How fascinating if we could actually do this"

At this point, Van Dijs, who has spent much of his career restoring mid-century houses in California, was only vaguely familiar with the Futuro Houses.

"I dug in a little bit, I started to learn about the history," he told Dezeen. "And I start to realise that it's something of a fascinating story."

"And I really had my doubts that all the pieces were there, that they could be restored, so I tried to keep all of that in check," he added. "But I certainly had started to make an emotional connection to how fascinating this could be if we could actually do this."

Twenty Futuro Houses had been fabricated in its native Finland originally, by plastics company PolyKem.

Exel had acquired PolyKem's assets, including the Futuro moulds, after the fabricator went bankrupt in the early 1990s – a difficult period for Suuronen that reportedly culminated in him and his wife losing their home.

In the decades since production stopped, the moulds had been periodically moved between various forms of storage without a purpose.

Suuronen died in 2013, and so once hooked on the Futuro story, Van Dijs spent several months trying to engage with the architect's family.

"I couldn't just buy the moulds and build this thing – I needed to have a license, and I needed to have their support," he said. "The reality was, unless I could do that, there was no future for this project."

The Suuronens were hesitant, having been contacted several times over the years about poorly thought-through schemes on a similar theme.

But eventually they were persuaded with help from the Exel man, Jyrki Aho, who died a short while later.

"The moulds looked like hell"

When Van Dijs flew out to see the moulds in May 2025, they were languishing in a field and nearly 60 years old.

"The exterior of the moulds looked like hell," he remembered. "I mean, there was grass growing out of them and moss covering them, and it looked really bad."

Nevertheless, the decision was made to proceed, and Van Dijs worked with Finnish plastic fabrication company Ekin Muovi to restore the moulds and recast the panels with the aim of producing a faithful reconstruction of Suuronen's design.

Even the same paint colours were used, having been matched from scraps that remained on the moulds.

It was a step into the unknown for Van Dijs, and he admits the process was trickier than he had anticipated.

While today plastic moulding uses two tessellating pieces – one to pour the cast into and one to press over it to squeeze out all the air – Suuronen's are one-part moulds, meaning air bubbles must be eliminated manually.

"It's all hand labour," said Van Dijs. "Nobody does it like that anymore."

Casting a single panel therefore took days instead of hours and was very labour-intensive – "no doubt a large contributor to the problems faced by the Futuro in the 1970s", Van Dijs suggests.

There were pleasant surprises as well, however. Unexpectedly, the moulds being sold by Exel included furniture designs by Suuronen, which have also been reproduced as part of the project.

They include built-in lounge chairs, a dining table, and the Orbit chair.

The fabrication process took five months, including some mishaps along the way. Including the restoration of the moulds, Van Dijs estimates the project has cost around 450,000 Euros, though he hopes further Futuros would cost less than 300,000.

In late June of this year, the 21st Futuro House to be made in its native country was completed, ready to be transported in several pieces for reassembly at its temporary home on the Kaisaniemi lawns.

For the Helsinki Design Week installation, Marimekko was invited to create an interior for the new Futuro House.

It opted to divide the open space into three areas – one for lounging and sleeping, one for eating and working, and a kitchenette.

"It was really important to sort of create a proposal for future ways of living," Marimekko creative director Rebekka Bay told Dezeen.

"That sounds like a big, grand statement, but we were really just intrigued by how we would live in the Futuro House today. I think there is a real trend for downscaling, and we felt that the Futuro House is sort of speaking to that."

Marimekko products were displayed on perspex shelving units that double as transparent room dividers, while stripy prints created for the brand during a residency by Danish textile artist Vibeke Rohland were used to upholster the furniture.

"It would have been obvious for us, of course, to go back to our archives and find prints that were designed in 1968 when the house was also designed," said Bay.

"But we wanted to take the opposite route and propose something that had been created today. We convey certain images when we speak to the future, but we wanted our proposal to be sort of tactile, lived-in, friendlier, and were therefore intrigued to use brand new textile designs."

With design week over, discussions about the structure's future are now ongoing, though Van Dijs said his preference is for it to remain on public display in Finland.

"I hope it will move somewhere into the countryside and someone will be using it as their summer cabin," said Bay. "I think that would be wonderful."

Van Dijs also plans to produce new Futuro Houses to order – but the run will be limited.

"Casting moulds are just like the plates for a print; they are designed for a limited number of editions," he said.

"I think the original moulds were probably near the end of their lifespan when production stopped. Through a significant effort we were able to extend their life, but not forever."

Read:

"What if houses were designed like bikes?"

He estimates that the restored moulds will support producing between four and six new Futuros. After that the moulds will be destroyed, and, in Van Dijs's words, "that will be the end of the original Futuros".

In his design, Suuronen focused on making the Futuro House quick to assemble, quick to heat and suitable for difficult terrains.

But it is also cramped, tricky to transport and dreadfully insulated, leaving it without an obvious practical use in 2026.

Nevertheless, Van Dijs is adamant that Suuronen's creation is more than mere whimsy.

"I would love to leave my home every day and go to my Futuro office, a small apartment, yoga studio, architectural book store," he suggested.

He regards the Futuro as an important touchstone for radical post-war optimism and creativity – the same conditions from which Marimekko was born in 1951 – and sees his project as a reigniting of that spirit.

"I think the Futuro should be considered an icon of Finnish design, which was not the case when it was originally produced," he said.

"This project allows us to see the Futuro as Matti Suuronen envisioned it – I think that's important."

Helsinki Design Week took place from 28 August to 6 September in various locations across Helsinki. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

Fifteen leading architects and designers met last week to decide the winners of Dezeen Awards 2026, in partnership with Trimble, which will be revealed at the Dezeen Awards 2026 party in November.

The master jury took place at the One Hundred Shoreditch hotel in London and included architects Ma Yansong and Daniel Libeskind as well as interior designers Wendy Saunders and Jaime Hayon.

Designers Martin Lotti and Jo Barnard, as well as architects Dominique Petit-Frère and Aziza Chaouni also joined to determine the 49 winning projects, ahead of next week's shortlist announcements between 21-23 September.

Winners announced at the Royal Opera House

All this year's winners will be announced at the Dezeen Awards 2026 party which takes place at the Royal Opera House in London on 16 November.

Guests at the party will be the first to find out who has won the prestigious project of the year awards across architecture, interiors and design. Tickets are available to purchase here.

Also unveiled at the ceremony will be the six winners of this year's Designers of the Year, who have each been shortlisted and selected by Dezeen's editorial team.

The Designers of the Year awards recognise the best emerging and established talent whose innovative work has made a notable impact on the industry across architecture, interiors and design.

"Designers thinking more critically about context"

The master jury discussed 392 shortlisted entries selected from over 4,300 projects in 91 countries around the globe.

Architectural designer John Cummins joined the architecture master jury panel which comprised architects Yansong, Libeskind, Chaouni and Petit-Frère.

Speaking to Dezeen, Petit-Frère observed how "this year's projects reflect a generation of designers thinking more critically about context, materiality, technology, and the social impact of what they create".

Hayon and Saunders were joined on the interiors master jury panel by Benni Allan, Julien Sebban and Bangalore-based Smita Thomas.

Thomas was also struck by the depth of this year's entries, which she saw as imbued with a sense of purpose rather than being solely aesthetic exercises.

"There were a number of projects that felt more like statements of intent than displays of style," she said.

"It charged me to see design beginning to shapeshift toward strengthening human connection in a time when we need it most," Thomas continued.

Parisian designer Sebban noted the "presence of so many young and emerging studios experimenting with new materials and new ways of thinking".

"The next generation is asking better questions, not just creating better answers"

Lotti and Barnard were alongside Michael Anastassiades, Min Chen and Alexie Sommer to decide the winners of the design categories.

Lotti, chief design officer at sportswear brand Nike, remarked that "the strongest projects weren't simply beautiful – they were purposeful, distinct and challenging the status quo".

"What struck me most was the range of thinking behind it. I came away feeling that the next generation is asking better questions, not just creating better answers," he continued.

Following the day of judging, an exclusive drinks reception and dinner took place in the One Hundred Room at One Hundred Shoreditch, where the master jury was joined by fellow 2026 judges Zandra Rhodes and Miminat Shodeinde.

Designers Paul Cocksedge, Ron Arad and Sebastian Cox also joined to celebrate the day's conclusion.

Following the shortlist announcements next week, the Dezeen Awards 2026 public vote will open and readers will be asked to vote for their favourite shortlisted projects. We will announce the public vote winners on Dezeen and across our social media channels ahead of the Dezeen Awards party on 16 November.

Tickets for the Dezeen Awards 2026 party are on sale. The occasion is an opportunity to celebrate with fellow nominees and VIPs, connect with others from around the world and reward your team for their hard work.

Studios that have been shortlisted for this year's Dezeen Awards will be eligible to purchase discounted tickets for £249. These tickets will be released on 21 September, alongside the shortlist announcements.

Subscribe to the Dezeen Awards newsletter to keep up to date with the latest announcements on the party.

Dezeen Awards is the ultimate accolade for architects and designers worldwide. The ninth edition of the annual awards is in partnership with global technology company Trimble. Through connected hardware and software solutions, Trimble helps designers to transform the way they shape spaces and buildings as well as drive productivity in the process. Trimble's collaboration with Dezeen Awards demonstrates its ongoing commitment to inspiring and supporting creative excellence across the globe.

item.content:encoded:
Promotion: in a time of dopamine design and AI tools, a group of design industry professionals at an Arca talk discussed what role colour is playing in the contemporary American home.

Colours such as olive greens and a shade called Black Martini are in, according to Tony Piloseno, owner of Orlando-based company Tonester Paints.

Piloseno joined interior designers Kati Curtis and Tamara Feldman for a conversation at Mexican stone company Arca's showroom in Miami, moderated by Dezeen US editor Ben Dreith.

And while the panellists agreed that rich, dark colours are in at the moment, the most important element of contemporary colour usage is about experience and reevaluating how people choose colour.

"I use tons of colour in my work, but what I'm thinking about, more so than trends, is how are we using colour?" said Curtis. "Are we using colour as an applied element, or is colour actually architecture?"

Both Curtis and Feldman referenced the work of Mexican modernist architect Luis Barragán in their framing of colour as more than a trendy accent.

"The term colour blocking has always bothered me because I feel like it's an accent – it's like putting wallpaper on one wall," continued Curtis. "It feels to me like you ran out of money, and you just went with that."

An expanded conception of colour utilises light, texture, and the aim should be to envelop whoever is in a space. The panellists noted how the presence of tinted glass in Miami makes this even more important.

This, for Feldman, means that the whole of an interior – including light – and all the way through to the artwork on the walls should work together.

"I don't think it's just about a colour and a wall," she said. "I think it's the whole concept together."

Feldman is currently designing a coffee pavilion for the Institute of Contemporary Art in Miami, where she has used mirrors and Arca's Umbria-fabricate tiles to create a sculptural work in the institution's gardens.

The idea that colour should envelop and create an emotional response has become a hot topic recently, with the emerging trend of so-called "dopamine design" seeing spaces covered in bright colours and mish-mashed patterns to stimulate the mind.

The panellists agreed that colour can work to make you feel at ease, comfortable or inspired, but that this is more related to individual preference and experience than any set configuration or style.

"Does the room look really cool on TikTok, then you hate it 15 minutes later because you threw it in there to try to create this cool picture?" asked Curtis. "It can definitely go in the wrong direction too if you don't know what you're doing."

Piloseno added that dark colours that wash over you can have a positive effect as well.

"There is a direct emotional impact that colour has, especially with these darker colours," he said.

The panellists also addressed AI in design, and how choosing a colour scheme can be risky. For example, once you apply the paint or veneer, it takes a significant amount of work to pivot in a different direction.

Visualisation tools have existed for years, but Curtis said that generative AI has allowed her to show clients what a space might look like more easily before they commit.

"Even if it's not an accurate representation of exactly what the colour is going to be, I think it's very helpful in giving clients an idea of the overall room rather than just testing a sample," said Curtis.

"What AI and just any kind of colour visualiser tool will help with is seeing the specific colour vertically or how it's going to look on the ceiling with specific shadows," added Piloseno.

Ultimately, though, the panellists agreed that the pursuit of colour, and whatever downstream emotional effects, requires a human touch.

"I think the whole process of selecting colours is very personal," said Piloseno. "You shouldn't have AI guide you to these specific colours."

The speakers added that personal relationships and understanding the emotions of clients are paramount.

Colour choices often represent this dynamic more than other aspects of design. If a designer is going to understand what will engage the mind, they need to know the mind in question.

"What we do is really part therapy, part design," said Feldman.

Technology underwrites the process while the person guides the choices on the table. And while neuroscience has created new streams for engaging with design schemes, Curtis said that the foundations remain as important as ever.

"As long as you stick with those fundamental elements that we all know, we can mix all of those things in a really beautiful way," added Feldman. "That's going to make everybody's dopamine work."

item.content:encoded:
A pasta-shaped daybed and speakers that resemble Saturn's rings are among the products on display at Contemporary Design Selections at this year's Lake Como Design Festival.

The eighth edition of the Contemporary Design Selections show, curated by Giovanna Massoni, follows the festival theme of Borders, encouraging participating designers, architects and makers to consider boundaries in design.

The theme could be interpreted through materiality, form, function or design's relation to other disciplines, while the open call also highlighted the social and political elements of the industry.

The exhibition is located at Villa Saporiti, which marks the first public showcase in the neoclassical building, and displays 57 projects by designers and studios from 30 countries.

The showcase features furniture, lighting, functional objects and textiles selected by Massoni across 10 rooms in the villa and its outdoor spaces.

Read on for seven design pieces that caught our attention:

Fur by Studio Bjorn Verlinde

Belgium-based Studio Bjorn Verlinde spotlighted its minimal Fur seating and side table collection at the exhibition.

Designed for restless people, the series features an unconventional backless rocking chair with a curved aluminium base that allows the user to gently lean back.

A contrasting seat made from brown leather sits atop the base of the chair, which is mirrored by the surface of the accompanying table.

Lights in Tension by Massimo Rigaglia

Massimo Rigaglia, a Milan-based artist and designer, created the Lights in Tension light collection from strips of flexible bamboo held in place by leather cords.

The result is a lightweight, curved structure anchored by a brass base that "embraces fragility as an aesthetic value", said Rigaglia.

BR Collection by Studio Alessandra Hofmann

These coffee tables by Basel-based Studio Alessandra Hofmann were informed by brutalist architecture.

The cube-shaped blocks of travertine are intersected with rectangular slabs of handmade cast glass, creating two levels to the tabletop.

The designer took an experimental approach to working with natural materials, embracing reactions created in the design process such as bubbles in the glass and open pores in the travertine.

Saturnia by ArmoniusLab

Founded by designer Elia Dusi, ArmoniusLab presented its Saturnia speakers, where the audio unit is encompassed by acid-treated iron that resembles Saturn's rings.

The speaker was designed to be placed on the floor and tilt upwards, so sound travels "not directly to the listener, but around the room," the studio explained, creating a different style of listening experience.

Tattile by Studio YellowDot x Artisia

Studio YellowDot collaborated with pasta company Barilla's 3D-printed pasta project Artisia to create a daybed that resembles the food's shape.

The hollow furniture, which was 3D printed in one piece from a wood fibre and bioplastic composition, features a ribbed surface similar to the pasta.

According to the studio, it responded to the festival's Borders theme by highlighting the border between food technology and design.

The Long Take by The Happy Few

This 10-metre-long wool rug by textile studio The Happy Few was designed to reflect the experience of walking down the street, with rectangular woven blocks resembling street tiles.

The designers sought to tell a story of seasonal changes through its colour palette, with shades of grey and blue transitioning to brown and green.

Claustra by What's Wrong Duo

Ceramics and furniture studio Whats Wrong Duo designed the Claustra room divider, which was informed by the soft lines and transparency found in the natural world.

Comprised of brown, purple, cream and grey hues, the furniture is made from aluminium and ceramic pieces, with the Bucharest- and Zurich-based studio also creating the glazes for the clay.

Through this design,the duo aimed to explore the boundary between a functional space divider and artistic expression.

The photography is by Sophie Chapman. 

Contemporary Design Selection is on show at Lake Como Design Festival from 12 to 20 September 2026.  See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.

item.content:encoded:
Local architecture studio Arquitectonica has shaped the MSC Cruise Terminal, the world's largest cruise terminal by size, in Miami to accommodate three ships at once.

Arquitectonica designed a slim, elongated building for the building, which processes 36,000 daily passengers through its 492,000-square-feet (45,700 square metres).

Arquitectonica has completed the world's largest cruise terminal at Port Miami

Its western end rises up to accommodate a grand lobby, with a mirrored peak rising away to hold the VIP lounges nearer the middle. The building then trails out in a thin tail, which holds embarkation and disembarkation gates.

It stretches along the easternmost tip of Dodge Island, which spans diagonally between Miami Beach and Downtown Miami and contains Port Miami, a long stretch of individual terminals that service Miami's many cruise companies.

The building's linear form was partially shaped by the need for organised and efficient loading, according to the team, "with minimal overlap or delay".

"Embarkation and debarkation are vertically organised, allowing both processes to occur simultaneously with minimal overlap or delay," said the team.

"This concept is reflected in the building's dynamic, linear form, which mirrors the directionality and movement of passengers and ships."

The terminal services ships from cruise companies MSC Cruises and Explora Journeys, both as a destination point for passengers exploring locally or cruises headed to the Caribbean.

The terminal is capable of accommodating, or berthing, three full-sized ships end-to-end simultaneously. Typically, while ports may see hundreds of ships pass through them each day, a terminal is capable of handling one mega-ship at a time.

The development also contains a 2,400-car parking garage for passengers.

Inside, the building rises to four storeys at its highest point, with a largely open interior with wooden walls, terrazzo floors, and wavy blue carpet. Gates, seating areas, and an enormous screen that casts an underwater scene fill the space.

It also contains biometric screening for passengers to "increase security and expedite movement", according to the team. 

Read:

World's largest cruise ship sets sail amid sustainability concerns

The project is pursuing LEED Gold certification with infrastructure to power future LNG vessels, ships that use liquefied natural gas instead of diesel.

The project broke ground in 2022 and officially opened in April 2025.

It joins another terminal at Port Miami for Virgin Voyages, also designed by Architectonica, completed in 2022.

"It joins a growing roster of recently completed cruise terminals at the port, further shaping the architectural identity of the Cruise Capital of the World," said the team. 

In 2024, the world's largest cruise ship set sail from Miami amid sustainability concerns surrounding the use of LNG, while the Frank Lloyd Wright Foundation announced cruises informed by the late architect last year.

The images are by Robin Hill, courtesy MSC Cruises.

Dezeen Showroom: economy of material and sculptural presence meet in this lounge chair, designed by Anne-Mette Bartholin and Morten Ernst for furniture brand Cozmo.

The Ginkgo lounge chair is the product of a simple gesture, where a 2D shape is turned into a 3D object using as little material as possible.

Bartholin and Ernst originally designed it in the early 2000s for then Danish manufacturer Weber Furniture. Bartholin worked with Cozmo for the last two years to update it for the present era, with consideration to proportion, construction processes and the engineering of comfort.

Named for its resemblance to the fan-shaped leaf of the ginkgo tree, the chair consists of only two structural elements: the moulded plywood seat shell, available in either oak or walnut, and a slender three-legged tubular steel frame.

An easily removable upholstered cushion completes the lightweight, stackable chair, which Bartholin describes as having a poetic and embracing character.

"Together, the two elements create a construction that is both simple and expressive, in which every part has a clear purpose," said Bartholin.

"The generous proportions invite you to sit back and put your feet up, while the curved shell follows and carries the width of the body, creating a subtle sense of dynamic tension."

item.content:encoded:
Scottish ash joinery and clay plaster add warmth to the granite walls of this low-lying extension to Cairngorm Cottage in Scotland, designed by local studio Architecture Office.

The extension was built for a client who wanted more space to host their extended family at their Victorian home in rural Aberdeenshire, all while retaining its cosy, contextual feel.

To achieve this, Architecture Office modelled the addition on the original low-lying cottage's design and prioritised locally sourced materials.

"The clients wanted to create more space for their extended family while retaining the intimacy and character of the original cottage," said studio director Alexander Mackison.

"The main challenge was designing a space that retained intimacy and character without becoming spatially dense or dark," Mackison told Dezeen.

"We were interested in what gives a cottage its particular identity. Modest scale, shelter, thick walls, deep openings and material character. The extension carries these qualities into a light space."

The Cairngorm Cottage extension replaces a small and dark addition made to the building in the 1970s. It contains a kitchen, dining room, utility and entrance hall.

According to the studio, the extension is oriented so that its longest facade opens onto the garden, making it "an intermediate space between the existing cottage and the landscape".

Externally, the extension's granite walls, coursing and deep-set windows echo the original cottage, as well as other buildings nearby in Cairngorms National Park.

The granite was reclaimed, with each piece chosen for its variation in colour and size. Lime mortar with a traditional Scottish slaistered finish – in which mortar is generously smeared – creates what Architecture Office called a "continuous, monolithic quality".

These heavy walls are visually lightened with crisp aluminium coping, drainpipes and vents.

"The existing architecture has a language defined by mass and solidity," said Mackison.

"We were interested in translating these qualities into a contemporary addition rather than directly reproducing the existing. As a result, there is a strong yet subtle relationship between old and new."

Read:

Loader Monteith rebuilds ruined Highlands house with blackened-larch extension

Inside, the home's layout has been reconfigured to ensure clearer routes between living spaces and to maximise views of the natural landscape.

Interior finishes are deliberately lighter and warmer than the cottage's exterior, with clay plaster and Scottish ash joinery used throughout.

The joinery was designed by Architecture Office and fabricated by Scottish furniture maker Silvan Studio.

This includes the home's focal point, its kitchen, in which units are arranged around a central island. The units are combined with oak flooring and Yorkshire stone worktops.

"To balance this massive exterior architectural language, the interiors are lighter but remain characterful," Mackison explained.

"The subtle tonal and textural variations of the clay plaster, paired with the grain and variation of the Scottish ash joinery, bring a softness and human quality to the house."

Other Scottish cottages recently featured include Dulnain, which Loader Monteith divided into two distinct wings using contrasting materials, and Iorram, which Baillie Baillie Architects filled with a natural palette of local materials.

The photography is by Richard Gaston.

item.content:encoded:
Kitchen brand Sage Appliances has launched a toaster that uses sensors to measure colour change to determine when toast is cooked.

Described by the brand as "a breakthrough in toasting innovation", the appliance allows users to determine how dark a piece of toast should be, rather than select the time that the toaster runs for.

When the toast reaches the required darkness, the toaster automatically ejects the toast, in theory making burnt toast a thing of the past.

"Time is the wrong metric," Sage Appliances head of research Tom Groundes-Peace told Dezeen.  "When we first started working on this project, we realised that there was a problem with all toasters – every toaster in the world's underlying technology works in the same way, it relies on a time."

As the Eye Q toaster uses a pair of sensors to determine when the toast is done, no adjustment is needed for different thicknesses or types of bread, and in theory burning is impossible.

Sage Appliances aimed to ensure that the toaster worked with all types of bread – from white to rye, with dedicated sourdough and crumpet settings. According to Groundes-Peace, sourdough's often-burnt crust and fluffy interior was the biggest challenge for the toaster.

"Different breads take different amounts of time to toast," said Groundes-Peace. "So a timer is not the best way to toast."

"The reason why we chose colour is that that's how you or I work out whether our toast is done," he continued. "We just look at it, and visually we'll know if it's done to our liking. Hence the name of the product, the Eye Q."

The sensors inside the toaster, which are patent-protected, monitor the toast up to 10 times a second to sense when the toast has reached the required level of colour.

According to Sage Appliances, developing sensors to monitor colour change that would work within the hot environment of the toaster was the biggest challenge for the creation of the appliance.

Read:

Kasey Hou aims to reduce electrical waste with flat-pack repairable toaster

"There was no componentry around available to do optical sensing for the format that we wanted, which is detecting food colour change – it just didn't exist," said Groundes-Peace.

"Our component suppliers saw colour change as a challenge, and then we said, 'also, we're going to put it in a super hot environment, right in the middle of the toaster, and then toast it again and again with it, 10,000 times'."

The toaster has a simple design with a prominent start/stop button and a row of buttons to determine colour beneath. According to the brand, this interface was designed to be as simple as possible as, in general, people won't need to adjust the settings often.

"The thing that stands out is the start-stop button, and really that's all we want people to engage with," said Groundes-Peace.

"We think once you've chosen your shade setting, you're not going to adjust it. You stick on the shade setting you like, and then every day you are just pushing that big button, and that's the simplicity," he continued. "Complexity is what happens underneath, but consumers don't even know."

Along with the colour sensor, the futuristic toaster contains several other customer-friendly functions, including a mechanism that lowers and raises the toast.

It also has a single-piece, non-stick ceramic-coated top to make cleaning easier and a retractable cable so that the length can easily be adjusted.

The photography is courtesy of Sage Appliances.

item.content:encoded:
British-Nigerian designer Yinka Ilori has designed a collection of bins, ironing board covers and kitchenware for home product brand Brabantia.

Named simply the Home Collection, the range was design by Ilori to add colour and joy to everyday items in the home.

"For me, the whole idea was to find the magic in the everyday," Ilori told Dezeen. "We put so much emphasis on the design of luxury and collectible objects, but often disregard the items we use multiple times a day – I wanted to shift that focus."

"We all have these daily rituals and routines, and the objects we use become such a big part of our lives, so why shouldn't they bring us a little joy? With Brabantia, I wanted to take these familiar, functional objects and give them personality, colour and a sense of play."

Ilori designed a trio of bins for Brabantia – a dual bin on legs, and five litre and 30 litre pedal bins.

The range also includes an ironing board and two additional covers, a drying rack and a gift set containing a water bottle, breakfast bowl and salad bowl.

All of the pieces are covered in Ilori's signature patterning and bright colours. The bins and the ironing board covers share a motif that begins as multiple orange lines before becoming a unified striped pattern.

"The artwork represents lots of individual efforts eventually coming together to form one bigger picture, much like the life you create," said Ilori.

Read:

Yinka Ilori's Dunelm collection aims to make good design "a lot more accessible"

"That's why the lines at the top feel more individual, before gradually connecting into a continuous pattern towards the bottom to create a joyful whole," he continued.

"As so often, I work with contrasting colours, in this case yellow, orange and purple, to create a real sense of rhythm and movement. I wanted each piece to feel like it had its own persona, while still feeling like part of the same family."

According to Ilori, bins were a perfect medium for his playful makeover.

"We spend so much time with these objects, often without really thinking about them, so I loved the idea of giving them a bit more inner life," he said. "Think of it as being the curator of your own home and placing artworks in unexpected places."

"If putting the ironing board up or displaying your bin can make you smile, that can elevate your day. I like taking something ordinary and creating a moment where people can experience a little bit of fun, even in the most mundane parts of the day," he continued.

"Plus, I genuinely love ironing. I find it very soothing, so applying my artwork to an ironing board felt like a natural extension of that."

Asked what would be the logical conclusion of his mission to add joy to mundane items, the designer suggested that his next project could be a toilet brush.

"The toilet brush," he said. "Definitely the toilet brush. I think we've found our next project!"

The collection for Brabantia complements a wider homeware and furniture collection Ilori recently created for department store Dunelm. Other recent designs by the designer include a Man of the Match trophy for the Africa Cup of Nations and an installation for Veuve Clicquot.

Dezeen Showroom: designer Sebastian Herkner worked with Italian heating brand Tubes to create Terre, the company's first radiator made from terracotta.

Taking its name from the Italian word for "earth", Terre is made from the clay of the Impruneta quarry in Tuscany, providing a warm, rustic contrast to the usual metal character of radiators.

Tubes used terracotta not just for the surface but as the structural body of the radiator, with the material being extruded through a special mould to achieve its continuous, long, vertical form.

The terracotta is fired and glazed with a choice of one of five glossy colours – including a transparent option that showcase's the material's natural character – and contains an integrated electric heating element made of recycled aluminium.

"I like exploring new methods and using a traditional, almost archaic material in a new context," said Herkner. "Terracotta is an authentic material, connected to earth and warmth."

"Using it today in a heating object creates a natural connection between function and material," he continued.

The Terre radiator is available with two optional accessories – a marble or lacquered shelf that lets the radiator double as a multifunctional catch-all in a hallway, and a metal towel rail that turns it into a towel warmer for the bathroom.

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studios RSHP  and ERRE have unveiled their plans for Valencia Central Station in Spain, which will incorporate public green spaces and sweeping roof canopies.

Designed by RSHP and ERRE with engineering firm Sener, the station will become the city's key rail hub, with connections to the existing North Station.

It will incorporate high-speed, commuter and metro services below ground, freeing up space at ground level for a linear public park the team described as a "green axis".

"By taking the tracks underground, we have the opportunity to reverse that condition and give the space back to people, creating new areas for walking, cycling, greenery and public life," ERRE told Dezeen.

"Burying the tracks that enter the city will be transformational for Valencia, allowing the city to reconnect," added RSHP director Simon Smithson.

Renders reveal Valencia Central Station as a wall-less structure sheltered by a series of sweeping roof canopies, reminiscent of the historic North Station.

Utilising a frame that filters light and air into the platforms below, RSHP and ERRE said the design aims to make the building "feel like it isn't underground".

Above ground, a public square will connect the station to the existing North Station, which is also set to be refurbished as part of the development.

Read:

Construction photos reveal progress on giant HS2 station by WilkinsonEyre

"For us, one of the most important gestures is simply to give it space," ERRE project architects explained.

"By opening up its facades and creating a new public square between the two stations, the historic building can breathe again and recover its full presence within the city," they added.

"We focused on opening the station box as much as possible to provide daylight, natural ventilation and views out of the deepest platforms," RSHP associate director Ainhoa Abreu Diaz said.

According to Diaz, a modular construction system will be utilised to speed up the station's construction process, though the completion date is yet to be disclosed.

"As with so many of our projects, for Valencia we propose a lightweight modular canopy and highly systemised station," she said.

"This will speed construction, minimise impact on neighbours, reduce construction waste, support principles of circular economy and allow us to target significant whole life carbon reductions."

Other stations recently featured on Dezeen include a metro station in São Paulo updated by local studio Nitsche Arquitetos and the Old Oak Common station in London by WilkinsonEyre, which is under construction as part of the HS2.

Over 30 designers, makers and studios have created limited-edition and prototype furniture and objects for Lobby, a new design platform launched by recruitment agency Collate Form during London Design Festival.

Collate Lobby's debut exhibition takes the form of a fictional hotel suite and foyer, inspired by the fashion and interiors of the 1930s.

Almost everything on show was developed by designers especially for Lobby, with standouts including a polished metal mirror by Jaclyn Pappalardo, a chainmail partition screen by Edward John Milton and a lounge chair by Matthew Coules.

The collection also includes small objects and accessories, including a lacquered resin lamp by Alexander Shayle, a cast bronze table lighter by Thomas Wheller, colourful silk scarves by Les Keepers and espresso cups by Maison S Sommet.

Founder James Garis conceived Lobby as a platform for emerging and established designers to develop new product concepts and test them on the market.

It is intended to be a platform that sits somewhere between a brand and a retailer, giving designers freedom to experiment but maintaining a degree of curation.

"I've met so many amazing, talented designers and makers over the years, but they have nowhere to funnel their work through in any sort of a controlled sense," Garis told Dezeen.

"There are services and websites that any decent designer can put their work on, but they aren't curated, so it never feels like a brand," he said.

Lobby's model differs in that, for each product drop, participating designers and makers are asked to respond to a distinct theme.

For the inaugural drop, Garis asked for an object that deserves to live in a Parisian "boudoir-like" hotel. He then worked closely with participants on the final stages of product development.

Read:

London has "the best architecture and interior design community in Europe" says Duncan Riches

All objects are available to order, with Lobby holding exclusive rights for a minimum of three years.

Those that prove most successful will become part of Lobby's core collection.

"So many people in the industry get screwed over by brands, but we're trying to be as fair as possible," said Garis.

"I'm not a designer, but I am a furniture geek, and I understand what sells," he added. "[This model] gives me a chance to see what I can do for these designers, and if it doesn't work, then they can take the idea somewhere else."

Lobby is presenting its debut exhibition at Yorkton Workshops, the home of design studio Pearson Lloyd. Spread across two rooms, it includes a reception area, a lounge space and a bedroom.

More than 40 objects are presented across these different areas, with key themes including art-deco style and material experimentation.

One example of this is Josh Page's Acid floor lamp, which combines a base of carved teak-veneer plywood and a poplin shade with a blue embroidered seam.

Others include Charlie Humble Thomas' Fred lamps, which pair sculptural blown-glass shades with blocks of polished British marble, and Odd Universe's tetris-like aluminium side tables.

Other notable pieces include a textile wall hanging by Andrew Pierce Scott, a pair of tassel pendulums by Christopher Kelly, oak stools with pewter inlays by Theodóra Alfreðsdóttir and textured ceramic sconces by Stine Keinicke.

Lobby is on show at Yorkton Workshops in Hackney from 12 to 20 September as part of London Design Festival. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

item.content:encoded:
Craft has become cool, while industrial design has lost its sparkle. What's driving the trend? And are they really so different? Debika Ray reports.

'Handmade', 'heritage', 'bespoke' – most of us are used to reading these words by now. Just like the food industry before it, the world of design has internalised the language of craft – that of the 'local', 'artisanal' and 'authentic'.

At London Design Festival (LDF) this year, exhibitions of craft abound.

These range from Reviving Craft at Somerset House, a show of more than 60 artisans from China curated by Beijing-based media entrepreneur Yang Lan to "create a dialogue between traditional craftsmanship and contemporary design", to Wood for the Trees at the Tab Centre in Shoreditch, an "abstracted woodland" in which to contemplate responsible forestry, designed by London-based Mitre & Mondays for the American Hardwood Export Council.

From Milan to Copenhagen, it's the same story: where once objects on display were proudly modernist, minimalist, sleek and uniform, they are now just as likely to be textured and imperfect.

The growing status of collectible design is part of the same movement – the desire for unique objects met by the inherent unpredictability of the human hand.

Pavel Klimczak, founder of design retailer Monologue London, has noticed this desire in the questions his customers now ask him.

"People are becoming much more curious about the stories behind objects," he said. "They often come for the design, but quickly the conversation turns to them asking where a piece was made, who made it, how it was made, why it was designed that way and the material used."

Craft was once dowdy. Now it's cool. And industrial design – that 20th-century emblem of democratised mass production, functional innovation and accessible beauty – has, whether fairly or unfairly, somewhat lost its sheen.

What underlying social and economic tensions does this shift reveal? And, beyond face value, is the line between 'craft' and 'design' especially meaningful in the first place?

"It's built on solid foundations"

The growing interest in craft is often attributed to our modern condition: the frictionless and ephemeral nature of our daily interactions, the cold dead pieces of technology we're continuously pawing, the deceptive nature of digital content, and the stylistic uniformity imposed over decades by globalised mass production and online connectivity.

In that context, it's no surprise we're drawn to unique objects that carry traces of human intention, are made of materials we recognise and are connected to a time, person and place.

A greater interest in the local, in heritage and in the vernacular also tracks with the current political mood: the simultaneous return, globally, of traditional values and a growing focus on cultures that have long been marginalised by modernisation and globalisation.

London Craft Week founder Guy Salter is convinced that our renewed interest in craft is here to stay.

"It's not going anywhere soon, as it's built on solid foundations – on more than just fashionability," he said. "We're rediscovering [things about quality of workmanship] that our forefathers knew for hundreds of years."

"And whenever I travel, I meet people who aren't attracted by the glossiness of luxury brands, but instead feel pleased to be supporting craft on a community basis."

Drawing on this interest, London Craft Week (pictured top) now attracts about 250,000 visitors every year – up from about 35,000 a decade ago – which compares robustly to LDF's 475,000 in 2025.

This year, in a boost for its credentials, fashion designer Jonathan Anderson – who set up the €50,000 Loewe Craft Prize while creative director of the Spanish luxury house – came on board as a sponsor via his own brand, JW Anderson.

Alberto Merlo Carrero, Loewe Foundation's head of programmes, says the founding of the prize in 2016 was a recognition that contemporary craft was on the ascent.

"Extraordinary work was already happening around the world, yet the field remained relatively fragmented and often underrepresented within the broader cultural conversation," he said.

Fashion brands from Hermès to Gucci now more often than not tend to showcase craft in their increasingly visible presence at design weeks.

"We're drowning in products"

Fostering a healthy craft ecosystem requires long-term commitment, which – more broadly – hasn't always been evident.

Salter says the expansion and corporatisation of the luxury sector in recent years has shaken up a business model that a century ago was mostly based on "a small number of customers buying or commissioning from what were often family-owned luxury shops".

In the process of trying to attract a mass audience, he explains, money was channelled into marketing via flagship stores and advertising, with craft often taking a hit – the in-house artisan replaced by outsourced production, for example.

"Now, a number of brands have realised what was lost during that period, especially during the recent downturn, and are trying to retrofit it," he said.

Against that backdrop, Salter says, craft has become a marker of quality and trustworthiness.

He adds that, while initially those new "aspirational customers" they were after took brands at their word, today's buyers are more discerning, and trust companies with a track record of standing by their values.

In contrast, industrial design is facing a "difficult predicament" as people increasingly question the ethics and purpose of mass production, according to London-based designer Lara Bohinc, who has collaborated with brands for decades and recently started working with clay.

"We're drowning in products. There are too many brands, too many chairs, too many beds," she said.

Meanwhile, cheaper design is often associated with bad labour practices, unsustainable processes or toxic materials – factors that are often ignored because these products are what most people can afford.

Calling something craft and charging a lot for it doesn't necessarily change the ethics behind an object, though.

Between 2023 and 2026, luxury fashion brands including Armani, Dior and Valentino were placed under court monitoring in Italy after investigations found they had outsourced production to illegal workshops where undocumented migrants were working under exploitative conditions on supposedly artisanal products.

"Just because it's handmade doesn't mean it's angelic," Bohinc points out.

"Few are making money exclusively from selling objects they've made"

Andu Masebo, a London designer who creates functional objects and art pieces in wood and metal, says he never had a "romantic notion" around craft – rather, he started making his designs simply because of the difficulty of finding a company willing to produce them for him.

He points out that the rise of craft isn't only a story about what consumers want, but also of what the industry is producing.

For designers, for example, the move to making is often driven by a fragile job market in which brands favour existing names over investing in new work, leaving emerging designers with few options but to produce things themselves.

"I feel like there could be a more positive conversation around how we create conditions that allow people to work in design and not just in the gallery space, and a concerted effort by the industry to reach out to emerging talent, not just as a marketing tool but as a way of supporting the future design pool," he said.

While craft may be in vogue, Masebo has observed that making itself doesn't necessarily offer a more sustainable livelihood than working for a design company.

"Few of my peers are making money exclusively from selling objects and furniture they've made," he said.

Instead, they use it to "express the highest version of their practice", while generating an income for themselves by diffusing that into a range of other related and unrelated sources, from social media to part-time jobs to commissions.

As Bohinc and Masebo highlight, categories such as craft and design may be useful from a marketing perspective, but underlying both are similar dynamics and challenges about quality, labour, employment and environmental impact that the sector cannot escape simply by changing how it describes work.

These extractive practices are among the subjects Nigerian-American designer Zoë Chinonso Ene is striving to address through her research and experiment-driven studio Homenkà.

In reality, she argues, craft and design aren't mutually exclusive categories, and the way we use those terms reveals underlying hierarchies in the value we place on different cultures of production – often based on aesthetic cues such as particular motifs, materials and styles.

"For example, with everyday objects from Igbo culture, I can see the decisions that were made to create object typologies for specific uses," said Ene, questioning why these are called craft rather than design.

Read:

How London designers are making it work

For LDF, Homenkà is creating an intervention as part of Brompton Design District – a parlour that will host evenings of play, eating, conversation and remembering "in the company of everyday design".

Its broader focus is on supporting craft ecosystems in Nigeria. In envisioning these, Ene isn't a purist about the separation between hand and machine.

"It may mean artisans working in a semi-industrialised space where they do 50 per cent, not 100 per cent, by hand, to speed it up while creating a fantastic product whose materials are sourced locally and gaining and exchanging skills," she said.

London designer Bethan Laura Wood has always straddled both worlds. She recalls that during her student days "craft was a dirty word in relation to design" – certainly not the case today.

For LDF, she is showing work as part of Craft x Tech, an exhibition by design studio Tangent that brings artisans from the Tōkai region of Japan together with international designers – in her case, to create folded hanging lamps made with shibori tie-dyeing company Suzusan.

Wood points out that public interest is like a pendulum – shifting from minimalism to maximalism, machine production to craft making – even as all these things continue to exist all at once.

The reactionary resurgence of craft is also not a new thing – think of the Arts and Crafts movement emerging in response to the industrial revolution, she adds.

That's not to dismiss the significance of what's happening now: waves of fashion can leave behind more substantive and meaningful change.

"When industry started to pay more attention to recyclability or circular design, some companies just flirted with those ideas to tick boxes, but others adopted it into their systems in a long-term way," said Wood.

Similarly, beautifully produced videos revealing the process behind objects – the metal spinning, the turning pots, the scraping of lathes – probably won't dominate social media algorithms forever.

But what might persist is a deeper concern among all of us about the provenance of the things we buy and a relationship between makers and designers that rewards both sides equally.

Promotion: Trimble SketchUp will bring its 3D Basecamp Summit to Las Vegas, exploring how artificial intelligence (AI) and reality capture are changing the way projects are designed, visualised and built.

Taking place from 9 to 11 November at The Venetian Resort in Las Vegas, the 3D Basecamp Summit will form part of Trimble Dimensions, a conference bringing together users of Trimble's technology across architecture, engineering and construction.

The three-day event will focus on the increasingly connected workflow between a designer's digital toolkit and the physical building site, combining hands-on workshops, technical sessions and talks from designers and industry experts.

One of the biggest themes will be the use of AI as a design tool, with sessions exploring how generative AI can automate repetitive modelling tasks while allowing designers to retain control over their work.

The programme will also look at how sketches and images can be converted into editable 3D geometry and how natural-language prompts can be used to generate models and tools.

The summit will examine how existing buildings can be brought into digital design workflows through reality capture such as scan-to-BIM, a process that uses scanning technology such as LiDAR to capture an existing physical environment and turn it into a digital model. This information can then be used alongside architectural models, connecting measurements taken on site with work being developed in the studio.

The summit will demonstrate how these models can move between the building site and design studio, rather than leaving information locked in separate silos.

The programme also covers interoperability between design, engineering and fabrication software, alongside extensions and coding that allow practices to customise their workflows.

Among the speakers is London-based interior designer Tola Ojuolape, who will discuss how she uses SketchUp to translate digital interiors into physical, material-led installations.

Ojuolape previously collaborated with Dezeen and SketchUp on a Design Workshop, using the software to develop a fictional three-storey library in London's Clerkenwell.

Other speakers include Jason Li of global workplace design practice M Moser and urban planner Devin Lavigne of Houseal Lavigne.

The summit will also include a panel moderated by Dezeen co-CEO Benedict Hobson, bringing together Ojuolape, M Moser and Programa to discuss the use of digital tools in commercial interiors and retail design.

The event will also feature the SketchUp Ascent Competition, where students and educators will present their 3D modelling projects live, with finalists pitching their work to an audience at Trimble Dimensions.

SketchUp is a 3D modelling platform used across architecture, interior design, engineering and construction. Trimble, which acquired SketchUp in 2012, develops software and hardware used across the built environment, including technologies for surveying, design, construction and asset management.

The 2026 3D Basecamp Summit takes place from 9 to 11 November at The Venetian Resort in Las Vegas and registration is now open.
