item.content:encoded:
Design student Gargi Agrawalla has won this year's UK James Dyson Award with a device that uses artificial intelligence to alert deaf and hard-of-hearing users of important sounds like knocks or fire alarms, which they might otherwise miss.

More than 500 samples were used to train the SIVO.GO system so it can recognise these noises and translate them into vibrations and flashing lights, rousing the user without the need for sound.

To design the alarm, the Loughborough University graduate drew on her own experience of being born profoundly deaf before receiving a cochlear implant at age 12. Although the implant allowed her to hear sounds for the first time, she discovered that its external sound processor had to be removed when sleeping or showering, which left her feeling uneasy in foreign environments.

"SIVO.GO came from my own experience as a deaf cochlear implant user and the anxiety I felt when travelling or staying somewhere unfamiliar," Agrawalla told Dezeen.

Existing alarms for the hard-of-hearing tend to be bulky and expensive, the student found.

Often, they are also geared towards only one particular sound like fire alarms or a crying baby, requiring users to pack a whole arsenal of gadgets when travelling.

"As a cochlear implant user, I already have to think about equipment such as chargers, a dry box and waterproof accessories, so adding several more safety devices creates extra stress," Agrawalla said.

"I wanted to reduce that burden by creating one portable system that could cover several important alerts and give deaf and hard-of-hearing users more reassurance when away from home."

Read:

Urify is a toilet-cleaning tablet that helps diagnose kidney disease

To achieve this, SIVO.GO uses an AI model trained on more than 500 sound samples, allowing it to distinguish between a range of different noises, from door bells to alarms.

This model is run locally on the device, rather than through Wi-Fi or the cloud, preserving user's privacy while ensuring reliability even in the absence of an internet connection.

To detect knocking or forced entry, the sound processor is also supported by a separate vibration sensor that can be attached to a door.

"During testing, door knocking caused too many false positives because the AI could confuse it with similar sounds such as footsteps or tapping on a table, even after adding more training samples," Agrawalla said.

"To solve this, I created a separate optional vibration sensor that can be mounted discreetly behind a door."

As the winner of the UK James Dyson Award, the graduate will receive a price fund of £5,000 to support the next stages of product development – improving reliability, expanding trials with deaf and hard-of-hearing users, and working towards certification and pilot manufacture.

"The same type of accessible alert system could also help people with tinnitus, neurodiverse users, exhausted new parents, older users, and even hearing people in situations where sound alone may not be enough," Agrawalla said.

The student will also be enter into contention to be crowned the international James Dyson Award winner, which in the past has included a gaming-inspired Parkinson's keyboard and an anti-hair loss helmet for chemo patients.

Promotion: furniture manufacturer Steelcase has unveiled its renewed WorkLife Studio space in London, which was designed to bring people and design expertise together.

The studio, located in London's vibrant Clerkenwell neighbourhood, aims to showcase the brand's latest workplace research and design solutions in an inspiring physical space.

Organic materials, including wood, were chosen to create a warm, welcoming interior, which is completed by a soft colour palette and plenty of green plants.

Steelcase said that the redesigned space now reflects the changing needs of today's workplace, which has been affected by increased screen time, shorter attention span, the rise of AI and a growing wellbeing crisis.

With WorkLife Studio, Steelcase aimed to create a space where people would be able to connect with each other and collaborate creatively.

"Visitors will discover seven interconnected zones, including collaborative neighbourhoods, technology-enabled meeting spaces, a co-design studio, a WorkCafé and flexible event areas," said Steelcase workplace strategy and design lead consultant Anisha Patel.

"The new space provides an opportunity to exchange ideas, discover the research and insights shaping the future of work, and experience first-hand how thoughtful design can enhance wellbeing, collaboration and performance."

Steelcase undertook extensive research and held design workshops to be able to tailor the WorkLife Studio to a range of styles and work preferences.

It now has focus areas for privacy and focused work, as well as collaborative spaces designed to encourage teamwork and a sense of belonging.

According to the brand, the aim is for the space to become a "living laboratory" where it can test new concepts and share insights together with customers.

Visitors to Steelcase's WorkLife Studio in Clerkenwell, which is now open, can collaborate with the brand's experts and see its products in action, as well as interact with a larger community of creators and designers.

item.content:encoded:
Local designer Veronica Mishaan has revamped a penthouse apartment with bursts of colour and animal prints in Bogotá, Colombia.

The 580-square-metre apartment was redesigned to balance the needs of the family with the ability to host, while preserving and displaying the clients' art and antiques collection.

"We aimed to preserve the essence of the space and keep alive the memories amassed over 30 years, while refreshing the palette of colour and materials and reworking the layout for a new era," Veronica Mishaan told Dezeen.

The apartment overlooks the city's greenery and mountainscape, so the design team worked to frame the views and bring the outdoors into the space with floral motifs, foliage tones and custom oak floors and finishes.

"Material choices, colours and window-oriented planning all reinforce the connection between the home and its natural context," said Mishaan. "We prioritised natural, tactile materials to reinforce warmth, longevity and a strong connection to the surrounding landscape."

Smooth marmorino plaster in the living room and circulation spaces serves as a soft backdrop for art. Grasscloth wallpaper carries through the dining room, primary bedroom and family room for a subtle texture.

Guests enter the apartment between an Elsa Foulon porcelain pendant and a staircase with a cast bronze railing that climbs like a tree branch through the apartment's multiple levels.

In the first living area, an antique Aubusson rug pairs with a custom Lee Jofa wool bouclé sofa, mid-century armchairs from Donzella, the studio's signature hammed iron martini tables and artwork by Peter Halley.

In the office space, the studio lacquered the original built-in bookcases and panelling in deep blue to complement the blue-leopard Stark carpet.

In the primary bedroom, Phillip Jeffries wallpaper envelops the room in rich indigo with pale blossoms that tie into the light pink of the patterned zellige travertine and marble tiles of the bathrooms. The team retained the original hand-painted sinks as a nod to the apartment's history.

The mirrored walls of the dressing room add lightness to the space with a parchment vanity and a curved bench upholstered in Pierre Frey velvet.

The dining room sets off an antique crystal and bronze chandelier with custom Schumacher light blue velvet dining chairs with leopard motifs and a soft coral wallpaper featuring tree branches.

Read:

Colombian designers transform Bogotá townhouse for furniture exhibition

Animal-print drapery hangs in the family room, tying together the dark blue walls, terracotta-toned sofa and sand hues of the artwork.

The team also created spaces that catered to the client's grandchildren with custom wooden bunks and a playroom with sage green millwork and bespoke children's furniture.

"What makes this project unique is the confident, successful juxtaposition of multiple patterns, colours and furniture languages to create a cohesive, layered whole," she said.

"That compositional balance, mixing antiques, contemporary art and locally made custom pieces, recurs throughout the apartment."

Mishaan said that the biggest lesson this project reinforced was not to follow trends.

"By prioritising lasting design principles, client needs, craft and locally made custom work, we produced a creative, authentic and unique home that will age well, a reminder to trust conviction over fashion in future projects."

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studio Grimshaw has released plans for a reimagined entry plaza for Allegiant Stadium in Las Vegas, transforming parking lots into transport infrastructure and walkways.

Grimshaw's plans for the redesign of the entryway mark both the city's commitment to the Boring Company's series of underground car tunnels and the move away from parking in the area adjacent to stadiums.

"Some of the most undervalued land in American sport and entertainment is the asphalt sitting empty immediately adjacent to venues that already draw the crowd," said Grimshaw partner Andrew Byrne.

The project will see the transformation of two parking lots next to the stadium into what is being called North Plaza.

Renderings show a platform raised to meet the road that overpasses interstate freeway I-15 and slopes down towards the current parking lots.

The platform will have large surface areas for gathering and be partially covered by a translucent canopy.

Underneath the canopy, a car lane will connect to Dean Martin Drive, which runs adjacent to I-15.

According to a Grimshaw spokesperson, the Boring Company station will be underground, similar to the station at the Las Vegas Convention Centre.

If it goes ahead, the station will be part of the broader Las Vegas Loop system, which currently has two underground stations that connect to the planned system of tunnels under the city. Only a fraction of the 65 approved miles of tunnel have been completed.

The Boring Company is owned by American businessman Elon Musk and uses Tesla electric cars to traverse the tunnels.

Formally, the North Plaza will look very similar to the black-clad Allegiant Stadium, which was designed by US architecture studio Manica Architecture and is the home of NFL team the Las Vegas Raiders.

At one end of the platform will be a circular structure. Byrne described the structure as a "placeholder" for a potential outdoor venue and shade structure.

Read:

Elon Musk claims Boring Company could build transatlantic tunnel for around $20 billion

A primary causeway underneath the platform will connect the stadium entrances with some of the remaining parking lots.

According to Grimshaw, the platform will serve both as an enhanced entryway and as a gathering place for fans.

Earlier this year, Dezeen took a look at modern stadium infrastructure in our Future Stadium series. Last year, the Boring Company was given a green light for a similar underground tunnel system in Dubai.

Dezeen Showroom: Felix Pöttinger Design Studio has combined a sculptural form and portable illumination in its Topo table lamp, created for German lighting brand Maytoni.

The Topo portable lamp combines a simple cylindrical base with a tiltable, disc-shaped shade. Its translucent diffuser creates a sharp interplay of light, shadow and reflection on the form below and casts soft atmospheric light beyond.

Portability is essential to the design of the rechargeable lamp, which was intended to look good in a variety of spaces and settings, from bedsides to shelf corners and outdoor tables.

"Topo is about creating a dialogue between light, surface and space," said Pöttinger. "Rather than treating the lamp as an isolated object, I wanted its presence to change depending on where and how it is used."

Compact and versatile, Topo is available in a selection of four finishes with a mid-century feel: black, light blue, brown and polished metal.

It is one of two portable table lamps created by Felix Pöttinger Design Studio with Maytoni alongside the battery-powered Asym.

item.content:encoded:
Timber shutters and the canopies of two large trees shade the interiors of House Beyond the Mango Trees, a home in Kerala by Indian practice InLe Architects.

InLe Architects founder Afiz Ubaid described the existing trees on the site in Kannur as its "biggest opportunity", providing shade and filtered sunlight while also buffering noise from a neighbouring highway.

"The challenge was the busy highway and the more urban context on either side of the site, while we were trying to achieve a calm atmosphere," Ubaid told Dezeen.

"Rather than simply accommodating the trees, we allowed them to influence the positioning of the house, the views and the experience of moving through the site," he added. "The controlled use of openings and filtered light was also inspired by the qualities we appreciate in traditional Kerala homes."

The entrance into the home is positioned between the two mango trees, forming the beginning of an axis that leads to a small courtyard and staircase at the opposite end.

In between, an elongated dining room sits at the heart of the home, opening out onto a small terrace to the north and connected directly to two ensuite bedrooms to the south.

At the eastern front of House Beyond the Mango Trees, the living space and kitchen on the ground floor and a study on the first floor overlook the trees through large, timber-framed windows, some of which are further protected by shutters.

Read:

Open-air temple sits beneath granite farmhouse on Kerala hillside

Two additional ensuite bedrooms are positioned on the southern side of the first floor, where they overlook the quieter edge and rear of the plot.

The internal finishes of the home were chosen to complement the dappled light passing through the trees, with pale plastered walls, stone floors and timber carpentry.

"The palette was kept deliberately restrained and calming. Since the clients will live with the house for a long time, we avoided bright colours and temporary trends, using neutral, muted tones and timber selectively for warmth," Ubaid explained.

"We wanted the materials to support the atmosphere of the house rather than compete for attention, allowing natural light, shadows and the changing presence of the trees to become more important," he added.

Other homes in Kerala recently featured on Dezeen include a stone home built into a steel hillside by Evolving Radical Aesthetics and a dwelling overlooking a lush cardamom plantation by Mindspark Architects.

item.content:encoded:
A new book from designer Adam Nathaniel Furman and Dezeen contributor Kate Mazade spotlights the most radical examples of colourful architecture from across history. Here, the authors pick six favourites.

Published by RIBA Publishing, Chromatic Architecture explores colour as an intrinsic element of architecture, rather than just decoration.

Across 34 examples, the book shows how colour has been used to convey emotion, memory or individuality.

"One of the biggest misconceptions of using colour in architecture is that it diminishes the seriousness or the purity of the design," said Mazade.

"We've worked to forefront case studies that use colour to reveal emotional depth, cultural understanding and an awareness of the places and people for which they were created."

The authors hope the book will encourage a greater appreciation for the role colour plays in shaping the character of the built environment, and offer a practical guide for architects and designers looking to introduce more colour into their work.

"There is a widely shared but rarely discussed love of colour amongst practitioners, and too often they feel unable to pursue that instinct," said Furman.

"The book was an opportunity to create a gentle and inviting manifesto, a cookbook of high-quality recipes, that creates a sense of permission to deploy beautifully crafted and well-considered chroma in projects," he told Dezeen.

Read on for six key examples of chromatic architecture, selected by the authors:

Shah Mosque, Isfahan, Iran, by Ali Akbar Isfahani, 1629

"This remains the ultimate reference for the use of glazed tiles to both dematerialise and define spatial volume," said Furman.

"The way the blue tiles map onto the complex geometric forms of the vaults and domes creates a sense of infinite expansion, seemingly revealing an entire cosmos of creation, showing how colour can manipulate our perception of space and our emotional response to it on a monumental scale."

Palau de la Música Catalana, Barcelona, Spain, by Lluís Domènech i Montaner, 1908

"Domènech i Montaner's use of mosaic, maiolica, stained glass, stone and brick here is a masterclass in total-work-of-art design," said Furman.

"It shows how colour can be used to dissolve the boundaries between the structure and the ornament, turning a public space into a jewel-box of materials, craft, light and pigment."

Guardian Building, Detroit, USA, by Wirt C Rowland, 1929

"This is an absolute masterpiece of art deco polychromy," said Furman.

"The way it uses glazed terracotta and stone to create a vibrating, rhythmic interior suggests that colour can function not just as an applied finish, but as an integral, structural element of a building's very soul."

Reversible Destiny Lofts, Tokyo, Japan, by Shusaku Arakawa and Madeline Gins, 2005

"The lofts are profoundly radical because they challenge the very notion that a home should be a neutral, fungible asset and backdrop," said Furman.

"By using a disorienting, high-contrast palette, they force the inhabitants to be physically and mentally present, proving that colour can act as a catalyst for human alertness and activity."

Netherlands Institute for Sound and Vision, Hilversum, Netherlands, by Neutelings Riedijk Architects, 2006

"Coloured glass offers an immense variety of hues across the entire facade of this major building," said Furman.

"It proves that architectural colour in a contemporary building can be both overwhelming in its intense effect and incredibly sophisticated in its depth."

Croydon Colonnade, London, UK, by Adam Nathaniel Furman, 2023

"My own contribution to the mix, this project focuses on the potential for handmade ceramics to bring vibrant, tactile colour to the public realm at immense scale," said Furman.

"It is a deliberate attempt to use saturated hues to transform a quotidian urban passage into a moment of collective joy and tactile, saturated architectural curiosity."

item.content:encoded:
Designer Jony Ive's studio LoveFrom has created its second collection for fashion brand Moncler, using symbols including its signature bear climbing the Empire State Building to celebrate the brand's flagship New York store.

The collection is organised around the down-filled Moncore jacket, which can be complemented by three interchangeable outer layers.

These consist of a parka, poncho and field jacket, which can be attached to the Moncore jacket using a magnetic Duo Button that Ive originally designed for the first LoveFrom Moncler collection.

The pieces, which have a soft beige colour, are made from recycled nylon. Their yarn-dyed fibres were air-textured to create a "soft, matte finish", the brand said.

Moncler weaves the fabric on extra-wide looms so each garment can be cut from a single continuous panel of fabric.

The LoveFrom-designed collection will launch exclusively at Moncler's new flagship store on Fifth Avenue in New York, the brand's largest ever, before being released globally.

Read:

First electric Ferrari launches with aerodynamic shell wrapped around sweeping glasshouse

To celebrate the city, Ive designed limited-edition New York City-inspired patches that can be added to the jackets – a yellow taxi, a guitar case, a drum set, an apple, a vinyl record and a bear paw print, nodding to LoveFrom's bear logo.

The collection also features a patch with a bear climbing the Empire State Building, and its packaging includes a set of nine New York-themed postcards.

Ive described working with Moncler CEO Remo Ruffini as "inspiring".

"Working with Remo is uniquely inspiring," Ive told Dezeen. "His understanding of the relationship between design, culture and place is extraordinary. It is an honour to make a small contribution to mark such a significant moment for Moncler in New York."

Ruffini has previously said of working with Ive that he "takes you out of the ordinary".

"Working with Jony is also an experience because you realise that love, friendship and respect are always at the centre and enable creativity and ideas," he said.

Ive is best known for his designs for technology brand Apple, but since leaving it in 2019, he has designed products in a number of different fields. Earlier this year, we rounded up nine of his non-Apple projects and revealed his and Marc Newson's design for the first electric Ferrari.

item.content:encoded:
As Shoreditch Design Week kicks off its inaugural edition at this year's London Design Festival, we interviewed creative director Duncan Riches about how he aims to bring design back to the east London neighbourhood.

If you ask people in London's design scene which of the ever-increasing London Design Festival (LDF) districts are a must-visit, chances are they'll say Brompton – where the V&A hub is – and Shoreditch.

The ex-industrial east London neighbourhood was the epicentre of the city's creative scene during the early 2000s, but has since become better known for its restaurants and nightlife – which seem to cater mostly to tourists – than its independent designers.

That could be about to change, though, as Riches, creative director of the newly minted Shoreditch Design Week, aims to help emerging designers and commercial brands work together to bring the design trade back to Shoreditch.

"I want to have a real core of trade"

The week will be centred around four curated trade exhibitions, including the interior design show House of Icon at Shoreditch Town Hall, graduate design showcase New Designers and materials fair Material Matters.

"I want to have a real core of trade; brands that show in the main venues, people from across London, hopefully companies from across the UK, and even better, companies not from the UK who want to work in the UK," Riches told Dezeen.

"I want to get those brands with their products in front of our audience – honestly, we have the best architecture and interior design community in the whole of Europe."

As well as the larger exhibitions, the week will also feature numerous smaller shows, while local brands such as Ally Capellino and Lee Broom will open up their showrooms to the public for product launches and drinks.

Riches's aim is for Shoreditch Design Week to become a place where "all the young talent and the emerging things can also have a home because really, what they all need is footfall and professional interest".

Shoreditch hospitality doesn't "have a relationship with the daytime economy"

But making Shoreditch fertile ground for designers once again is not without its challenges. Other popular design weeks, perhaps especially Copenhagen's 3 Days of Design, often integrate the entire neighbourhood, something that doesn't currently happen in Shoreditch.

"One of the problems in Shoreditch is there are so many restaurants and bars and a nighttime economy," Riches said.

"They don't have a relationship with the daytime economy. If you go to 3 Days, you'll go to a lovely showroom, you'll see some beautiful lights, and then the florist across the road has got the lights hanging there and the pastries are from the pastry shop next door."

Read:

London design "an international success story" says Sadiq Khan

In contrast, Shoreditch doesn't have those connections as the industries aren't working together, according to Riches, despite his various attempts to integrate them.

"I desperately tried to get a lovely restaurant last year to take out all of their furniture and put in Fredericia because they wanted to do a show there," he said.

"They were like, 'You're mad. What is this?' And then like four weeks before, they said, 'Oh, we think we could do that.' And I said, 'We need to know four months in advance."

With events company Media 10 having recently bought Shoreditch Design Week – formerly known as Shoreditch Design Triangle – from furniture brand SCP, Riches says the event now has access to larger spaces and is able to put on much bigger shows.

"What Media 10 do, and the investment that they bring, is multi-year deals," he said. "So when you go to Shoreditch Town Hall and say to them, 'Look, we want to do it for three years,' you get the kind of rate which allows you to put on a show and make it okay in terms of the cost for the exhibitors."

Industry-focused events lacking at LDF

Riches believes there is still a need for an event that is more focused on people working in the industry – something that he thinks is lacking when it comes to LDF as a whole.

"They've done a brilliant job in promoting design culture across London," he said. "But what happened is they've stopped serving the kind of core design community, and that is furniture, product, lighting, textiles, ceramics, glass – that kind of world."

"It's great that there's a platform for design, all types of design around London. But the people in the industry, they need an industry event; they need buyers to come, they need architects to come. They need both of them."

Riches believes that creating a trade hub in Shoreditch will also prove to be beneficial for the wider LDF event.

"I just hope that us being able to create a kind of trade epicentre, if you like, will really help LDF in general," he said.

And while he doesn't see Shoreditch Design Week as being a competitor to LDF, Riches also wants the area to have its own unique identity.

"We've called it 'Design Week', by the way," he said, "because it really does need to stand on its own two feet."

Riches hopes the mixed programme at this year's inaugural edition will mean that everyone can see something they're interested in – whether it's design industry people spending a whole day in the area, or people who just swing by an event after work.

As well as the main flagship shows, there are a number of younger designers showcasing their work, including design gallery Slancha.

"My job is like a massive matchmaker"

Riches sees facilitating collaborations between smaller designers and brands – such as Slancha's takeover of the shop at The Hoxton hotel this year – as a key part of his job.

"My role is to be a friend to everyone," he said. "Often brands are so wrapped up in the busyness of what they're doing, they find it hard to actually know who to go to or where to go. My job is like a massive matchmaker."

But there might be less need for design matchmaking in the future. Riches has found that emerging designers today are more capable of getting their work seen than in previous years, which he takes as a reassuring sign.

Read:

Five galleries injecting renewed energy into the London design scene

"If I take a young designer now and I look at their knowledge base, I think they're a lot more canny than they were 15 years ago," he said.

Overall, he believes that the current London design scene is also more vibrant than it has been in many years.

"There is loads to be really positive about right now, and I'm just amazed at where we're at," said Riches.

"And as a Londoner, I'm just kind of thrilled to come back, because London always has that up and down. It's always going to have that, but it feels like we're at the stage where it's just coming up once again, and there's a bit more excitement about it."

item.content:encoded:
Designer Lee Broom has created an "atmospheric environment" in his Shoreditch showroom with The Chant Chambers, an installation showcasing his glass-block Chant lighting collection at London Design Festival.

The Chant Chambers displays the modular light in a variety of forms – as a portable lamp, wall lamp, linear pendants and oversized chandeliers.

All are presented inside Broom's showroom, where textured vertical screens create a series of interconnected spaces designed to have a cinematic atmosphere.

The Chant Chambers, which Broom described as "an elegant yet surreal lounge," has wood-panelled walls and tactile wall-to-wall carpeting and features stone plinths and a number of sculptures.

"I wanted the Chant Chambers to feel like an atmospheric environment rather than a display of individual lights," Broom told Dezeen.

"The installation explores how the same cubic form can be transformed as it is repeated across a space, using different configurations to create a sense of discovery," he continued.

"It also reflects the way our clients are looking for lighting that can be adapted specifically to their interiors rather than choosing a single fixed object."

Broom also used Chant lights in linear arrangements as geometric ceiling designs with an architectural feel.

The moody, smoky colour palette of the installation was inspired by Chant's latest iteration – a smoked-glass finish in a darker tone than the previous design.

Read:

Lee Broom displays "sculptural tableau of light" for Mexico City art week debut

"The new smoked glass finish was a starting point for the concept," Broom said. "It has a depth and warmth that works particularly well with the design of Chant and it nods to the late 1970s, early 80s period when glass blocks were very prevalent in modern architecture."

"The palette was developed around those darker, richer tones to create a space that feels alluring and atmospheric, while still allowing the geometry of the lighting to stand out," he continued.

Glamorous 1970s interiors have been making a comeback, with a number of designers looking to the decade for their interiors, as seen recently in a Marseille wine bar.

Broom believes that his Chant light has played a part in this trend, especially when it comes to bringing geometric forms and glass blocks back into contemporary interiors.

"Since I first introduced the original Chant Chandelier in 2022, those references have gained real momentum," he said.

"What interests me is reinterpreting them rather than simply recreating the 1970s, giving those nostalgic materials a more contemporary expression."

He argues that these types of interiors also help put the focus on the lighting.

"This kind of aesthetic really allows lighting to take centre stage, not just through the fixtures themselves, but through the ambience they create," Broom said.

At the end of The Chant Chambers installation, Broom placed a three-tier Chant chandelier to fully showcase the lighting collection.

The designer has previously created a "sculptural tableau of light" for Mexico Design Week and a chandelier installation for last year's London Design Festival.

item.content:encoded:
Promotion: Italian company Lualdi has evolved its architectural door designs from the likes of Piero Lissoni and Kokaistudios to encompass partitioning and panelling systems, bringing sophistication and coherence to interior schemes.

Founded in 1860 as a carpentry shop and known in the 20th century for its interior doors, Lualdi has become increasingly ambitious in the expansiveness of its offerings, creating holistic systems used to organise spaces with elegance and clarity.

"As the boundaries between residential, hospitality and workplace spaces become increasingly blurred, interior architectural design is gradually shifting away from the notion of isolated objects towards integrated systems that coordinate space, functions and user experience," said Lualdi.

In response, the company said it had expanded the traditional concept of the door in recent years to encompass an "ecosystem" of integrated architectural elements.

With this way of thinking, the door becomes continuous with the surrounding structure, both receding into quietness and taking on a heightened grandeur.

"Doors, partitions, panelling and storage units become tools to create continuity, organise spaces and define new relationships between the various functions of the space," said Lualdi.

The flagship product of Lualdi's current era is Framework. Launched in 2025 and based on a design by the company's artistic director Piero Lissoni, Framework treats the wall as "a genuine architectural infrastructure", said Lualdi.

Built on the company's formal research and a new frame technology, Framework allows for the fixing of doors, panels and fronts along with functional accessories such as shelving.

Lualdi describes it as "a new concept of boiserie", referring to the characteristic French wall panelling, with a modern aesthetic and material palette of glass, metal, gloss lacquer, leather and woods.

The modular system allows for the creation of walk-in wardrobes, workspaces and other custom solutions while minimising the need for structural interventions. Lualdi explained it is also easily adapted to complex geometries.

"The result is a design platform that allows architects and interior designers to create rooms using a coherent language of surfaces, openings and functions," said Lualdi.

The Framework offering includes a new 61-millimetre door with an aluminium frame. The accessory options include illuminated shelves, open compartments, drawers and hanging rails, while the finishes include stained woods from bleached oak to fossil black oak and fluted or mesh glass.

A system, which can be used alone or also in combination with Framework, is Shoin, designed by Dante Bonuccelli. Informed by traditional Japanese houses and their sliding shoji paper room dividers, it features glass panels and doors with minimalist aluminium profiles.

Sliding and pivoting designs are available, and different types of glass – including satin-finished fluted designs and mesh-style Retina glass – help to balance openness and privacy while maintaining a flow of light.

Lissoni's L7 and L7 Bi-folding doors have a similar quality, helping to maintain visual continuity and a sense of lightness.

In Koan Light, an evolution of the Koan doors by Shanghai-based Italian designers Kokaistudios, the system combines glass and vertical wooden slats to create lightly drawn boundaries between rooms and give a calming balance between transparency and materiality.

Beyond glass, the Framework system offers the option to integrate stoneware, glass, faux leather or metal, turning partitions into a dynamic 3D surface enlivened with customisable metal inlays.

Lualdi's vision for contemporary interiors can be viewed in its new London showroom on Margaret Street in Fitzrovia, opened in May 2026.

Lualdi conceived the showroom as a workplace and venue for architects, interior designers and developers to exchange ideas, and used its panelling and partitioning systems to create a layout that invites exploration.

Hotelier Not A Hotel has revealed its latest guesthouse will take the form of a human-sized Pokémon Poké Ball, nestled beside a lake in Hokkaido, Japan.

Set to be built in Tomakomai City, the Poké Ball-Themed Hotel will feature a three-metre-diameter spherical guest room shaped like the balls used to catch and store wild creatures in the popular Pokémon game.

Designed by Not A Hotel's in-house team of architects, the structure will comprise two moulded acrylic hemispheres and a curved acrylic window, giving the appearance of an opening ball.

It will aim to immerse guests in both the natural setting and the world of Pokémon.

Visitors will enter the spherical structure through a sliding, curved door. Inside, a custom-designed circular mattress will fill most of the interior.

A washroom will be decorated in tiles the colour of the Snorlax – a Pokémon character known for its long sleeping habits. Guests will be able to select custom interior lighting themes based on Pokémon characters.

Read:

Iittala and Pokémon design stripy tableware emblazoned with Pikachu

"As society becomes increasingly convenient and efficient, Not A Hotel aims to bring more joy to individuals' lives," said Not A Hotel.

"For years, Pokémon fans have dreamed of stepping inside a Poké Ball," it continued. "Not A Hotel, leveraging its architectural and technological expertise, has turned that dream into a reality."

"This structure transcends the boundaries of architecture and product design, fusing the world of Pokémon with the architectural quality that defines Not A Hotel."

Created in collaboration with sleep-tracking game app Pokémon Sleep, the hotel will open in celebration of the third anniversary of Pokémon Sleep and the 30th anniversary of Pokémon this year.

Not A Hotel said people will get the chance to stay in the giant poké ball by winning an upcoming competition, but the room will not open to the public for bookings or visits.

Other projects by Not A Hotel that have featured on Dezeen include a coastal holiday home designed by Sou Fujimoto and a trio of rammed-earth villas designed by BIG.

Promotion: American furniture design brand Herman Miller has been honing its Aeron office chair for decades, equipping it with innovative materials and features for modern workplaces.

Featuring an ergonomic form that supports sitters of different sizes and technological enhancements for better long-term sitting, Aeron was first designed in 1994 by Bill Stumpf and Don Chadwick.

According to Herman Miller, its launch was revolutionary in the office furniture industry, and it continues to lead the charge, thanks to a timeless design informed by ongoing research and use of innovative materials.

"For decades, we've been perfecting it so that it's not only good for your body, but good for our environment too," says MillerKnoll vice president of sustainability, Gabe Wing.

"Aeron's launch was revolutionary in the office furniture industry, and it continues to lead the charge thanks to updated research, material innovation, and an iconic design that lasts."

The most recent iteration of Aeron is equipped with Herman Miller's patented 8Z Pellicle, an elastomeric suspension material designed to assist weight distribution. It features an adjustable back support system that helps encourage a healthy posture when sitting.

The chair's tilting motions also mirror the sitter's natural pivot points at the joints, moving with the body to help keep it relaxed.

Over 50 per cent of Aeron is constructed from recycled materials, including ocean-bound plastic waste, which Herman Miller has been incorporating into the design since 2021.

The ergonomic office chair comes in three sizes and is available in six colours that range from dark blacks and blues to varying tones of grey and an olive green.

"Aeron's material innovation is at the heart of its sustainability story, and a lesson in the major effects of dematerialisation," says Wing.

"Not only is Aeron actively innovated upon, but it's also naturally sustainable through its quality design, which keeps it out of landfills. When we say Aeron is a lasting design, we mean it wholeheartedly."

item.content:encoded:
Local studio Gonzalo Bardach Architecture has created a concrete house with shading screens and green roofs for "atmospheres that support everyday inhabitation with calm and depth" in Argentina.

The screens and filtration take on a central role for the house, both conceptually and in terms of light and privacy.

"Casa JR was conceived from the idea that architecture is defined as much by what it filters as by what it reveals," Gonzalo Bardach, founder of his eponymous studio, told Dezeen.

"This project explores a calm, horizontal way of living, where concrete, light, shadow and vegetation work together to create a series of intimate spaces."

"Rather than standing as an isolated object, the house seeks to become part of its surroundings, allowing everyday life to unfold in close relation with nature and the passage of time," he continued.

The 140-square-metre house was built in San Isidro in the Buenos Aires Province and is structured as a sequence of voids and solids.

The enclosed rooms alternate with a staircase courtyard, a 30-square-metre semi-covered porch and an upper terrace that regulate the relationship between the interior and exterior without rigid hierarchies, the studio explained.

The square house is offset on the densely vegetated site.

A walkway runs from the street along the side of the house to a side entrance in the centre.

An open kitchen, dining and living room takes up most of the ground floor, spilling out onto the shaded patio through floor-to-ceiling sliding glass doors.

The primary suite is on the other side of the ground floor and looks out at a rectangular pool.

Up the planted vertical circulation core, the secondary bedroom and a lounge space form an L-shaped second level that opens to a garden roof.

The house is composed entirely of sienna-toned concrete in smooth, board-formed and saw-tooth profiles that allow light and shadow to become part of the material palette with restrained timber and metal accents.

"Developed in a warm tone, close to that of earth and sunlight, [the concrete] allows for spaces where mass does not enclose, but protects, filters and creates intimacy," the studio said.

"Thick walls and filtering planes regulate views and establish a controlled relationship between inside and outside."

Read:

Studio Bright shades Melbourne home with metal screens for climbing plants

"Light enters indirectly, passing through filters, offsets and thicknesses that produce a continuous interplay between light and shadow," the team continued.

"These variations accompany the passage of the day and make time perceptible, generating atmospheres that are more experiential than formal."

The naturalistic planting strategy also filters the light, modulating views, generating shades, and creating microclimates in and around the house.

"Vegetation accompanies the architecture without dominating it, introducing seasonal variation and reinforcing the relationship with the environment," the studio said.

"The landscape does not act as a backdrop, but as an element that gradually transforms the perception of space."

The studio took a similar approach of natural integration for its Forest House in Costa Esmeralda.

Other homes recently constructed in Argentina include a Buenos Aires home enclosed in a curving concrete wall by Ademas Arquitectura, a white modular house on stilts in the mountains of Cordoba by SET Arquitectura and the renovation of a compact 1950s house also in Buenos Aires by Estudio Futuro.

The photography is by César Béjar.

IE University

Institution: IE University
School: IE School of Architecture and Design
Course: Master in Interior Design
Tutor: Andrea Caruso

School statement:

"IE School of Architecture and Design, part of IE University, brings together architecture, design, fashion and related creative disciplines across its Bachelor's and Master's programs.

"With an international outlook, the school offers a diverse educational environment that connects creative disciplines with the wider cultural, technological and business landscape.

"The school's master's portfolio spans architecture, interior design, immersive experiences, real estate development and business for architecture and design.

"Across these fields, programs combine creative thinking with practical knowledge, encouraging students to respond to evolving professional and societal challenges.

"The Master in Interior Design takes a holistic approach to spatial design, combining design development with sustainability, craft, technology, business and user experience.

"Based in Madrid, the ten-month program encourages students to consider how interiors influence wellbeing, behaviour, identity and everyday life.

"Students work through practical projects and industry-informed briefs, developing solutions that respond to real contexts and client needs.

"Across the school, IE emphasises learning by doing, interdisciplinary collaboration and engagement with professionals.

"This approach allows students to develop not only creative and technical capabilities, but also the strategic and entrepreneurial mindset needed to lead within contemporary architecture and design."

Healing the Ruin: Medicinal Planting and Hydrological Systems at the Renwick Smallpox Hospital by Nyah Nassif

"Healing the Ruin reimagines the abandoned Renwick Smallpox Hospital on Roosevelt Island as a living hydrological system, reactivating the building's original gravity-fed water infrastructure to cultivate seven medicinal and toxic plants through misting and rain-harvesting.

"Drawing on Derrida's notion of the pharmakon (substances that both heal and harm) and on hauntology, this proposal lets decay and cure coexist within the same structure rather than erasing the ruin."

Student: Nyah Nassif
Tutor: Andrea Muniáin

Territories of Care: Regenerating Lake San Pablo by Isabel Dorn

"Territories of Care confronts the looming ecological collapse of Lake San Pablo in Otavalo, Ecuador.

"Built from local bahareque and typha thatch, a family of modular structures threads along the shoreline, water-treatment plants, chinampas, drying racks, fish farms and floating algae platforms, which purify the lake while producing food, framing gastronomy and craft as tools of regeneration."

Student: Isabel Dorn
Tutor: Fernando Pino

Edible Commons: Spatial Systems for Collective Kitchens by Arianna Castro

"Edible Commons investigates the ollas comunes, the self-organised collective kitchens of Pachacamac on Lima's periphery, treating food access as a spatial rather than purely social issue.

"Its 'Scaffold Commons' is a scalable, modular system built from low-cost, reused and local materials, working across three levels (Adaptation, Co-creation, and Fabrication) to help communities improve cooking, storage and gathering conditions."

Student: Arianna Castro
Tutor: Jerónimo van Schendel

Above La Paz by Vasco Amado

"Above La Paz proposes a new typology of care on the rooftop of Hospital La Paz's oncology department in Madrid, addressing needs that clinical environments rarely meet.

"Drawing on the greenhouse as an archetype, it develops a modular timber system of four spaces (care, connection, threshold, intimacy) with a living tree nursery that uses daylight and seasonal rhythm to support patient wellbeing."

Student: Vasco Amado
Tutor: Paula Montoya

Third House: A New Music and Dance Residency & School for Migrant Minors by Lila Gaffney

"Third House transforms the Pavillon du Lac, a vacant 1863 pavilion in Marseille's Parc Borély, into a residential music and dance school for unaccompanied migrant minors awaiting minority trials and placement.

"A modular construction system inserts sleeping units, practice rooms, and performance spaces into the historic building, turning an unavoidable period of waiting into one of belonging."

Student: Lila Gaffney
Tutor: Fernando Pino

Reimagining Passive Waiting in Dubai International Airport by Aishwarya Geetharani

"This project reimagines the draining experience of waiting at Dubai International Airport Terminal 3, taking the jet bridge, the one space every passenger passes through, as its site.

"Drawing on Emirati architectural traditions, three modular configurations each cultivate a distinct state, Solitude (I), Resonance (V), and Reverie (X), using calibrated light, sound, smell and touch to give travellers more agency over how they wait."

Student: Aishwarya Geetharani
Tutor: Jerónimo van Schendel

Between Threads: How Can Fragmented Textile Practices Rebuild Community in Lucre? by Francesca Torres

"Between Threads addresses the fragmentation of textile practices in Lucre, Cusco, once home to Peru's first modern textile factory, where centralised production collapsed, but weaving endures, dispersed across households.

"Instead of introducing new activity, the project embeds a lightweight spatial system in the domestic threshold, community-built from local eucalyptus and rope, that lets homes work as connected spaces for production, learning and community life."

Student: Francesca Torres
Tutor: Paula Montoya

The Evolutionary Frequency: Suturing Soundscapes at Escudo de Veraguas Island by Ismela Marie Ruiz

"Escudo de Veraguas, a protected Panamanian island and one of the Caribbean's most biodiverse ecosystems, was closed by the government in 2024 after ecological violations, illegal construction, overfishing and noise pollution that displaced its Indigenous Ngöbe-Buglé community.

"The thesis asks how the Ngöbe-Buglé can guard the island's recovery through sound, proposing demountable tensegrity speaker structures for reefs, mangroves and forest that broadcast restorative soundscapes while combining ecological monitoring and community ritual."

Student: Ismela Marie Ruiz
Tutor: Andrea Muniáin

Life in Plastic: The Undesigned Interior by Camila Chahin

"In flood-prone Honduras, where storms like Mitch, Eta and Iota recur every few years, water is a permanent condition of domestic life rather than an accident.

"Instead of rebuilding after each flood, the project adds a flood-adaptive interior layer to the existing home, reimagining familiar furniture (beds, wardrobes, tables, refrigerators) in washable, buoyant plastic so households can adapt in place and keep the right to stay."

Student: Camila Chahin
Tutors: Andrea Muniáin

Territory Becomes Object Becomes Territory Again: The Gaucho as a Landscape Infrastructure by Carolina Estelles

"The project reimagines the gaucho as an agent of ecological repair in Argentina's Pampa Deprimida, along the Salado River.

"A nomadic, biodegradable module, built from local materials (willow branches, acacia thorns, reed fibre and cow bone) and seeded with native species, is carried on horseback and dispersed across the basin by cattle, regenerating degraded soil and wetland over decades."

Student: Carolina Estelles
Tutors: Andrea Muniáin

item.content:encoded:
Trapezoidal motifs appear throughout this concrete condominium block in Tokyo, designed by Japanese studio Ryuichi Sasaki Architecture.

Named Shin Nakano Trapezoidal, the five-storey block of 11 residential units was designed for local developer Real Partners.

According to Ryuichi Sasaki Architecture, the angular, trapezoidal motifs that feature throughout the design were informed by the project's location on the Musashino Plateau, a large tableland in western Tokyo.

"The Musashino Plateau is one of those landscapes that people live on without ever seeing," said principal architect Ryuichi Sasaki told Dezeen.

"Our challenge was to take something as abstract as a position within a plateau and translate it into a motif that residents encounter every day," he continued.

"[It is] in the facade they walk past, in the shadows on the stairs, in the light that reaches their rooms."

On the block's eastern edge, a sheltered entrance area is framed by tall, trapezoidal concrete columns and features trapezoidal floor tiles.

A large sliding metal door leads into a lobby and stairwell, where an industrial-feeling steel staircase with grille treads allows daylight to filter through.

This lobby divides the block into three wings across which the apartments are separated, with a combination of single-storey and duplex units that extend into a basement and rooftop terrace.

Each apartment takes advantage of views over the street to the south and a park to the north, with large metal-framed windows that slide open for cross-ventilation.

The interiors are deliberately minimal and pared-back, with timber floors, exposed concrete ceilings, white-painted walls and large areas of built-in storage.

Read:

Groupwork completes "world-first" high-rise held up by stone exoskeleton

The trapezoidal motif was carried through into openings in the interior walls and floors, staircase balustrades and even the floor plan of some rooms.

Externally, the block is finished in exposed concrete, with textured trapezoidal and triangular panels created by embossing the surface of the concrete after it was poured.

"A residential building of this scale is experienced in fragments — an entrance, a stair, a window — so the motif had to work at every one of those moments," said Sasaki.

"We are proud to offer the residents of Nakano a building that connects them, quietly and daily, to the ground it stands on," he added.

Previous projects by Ryuichi Sasaki Architecture include a mixed-use development containing homes and a community performance space in Tokyo, which was housed within similarly angular concrete volumes.

Elsewhere in Tokyo, Kenta Hirayama recently created the steel-clad House in Kinuta and Kenta Sano & Associates combined a glass-fronted dance studio with a house.

item.content:encoded:
This year's London Design Festival landmark project, The Pangolin Shield, explores Britain and India's colonial history through a bamboo-grid pavilion covered with shields used both for protection and aggression.

Named after, and baring a resemblance to, a pangolin – a scaly mammal – the pavilion is located on the newly pedestrianised part of The Strand outside London's Somerset House and near India House. According to Studio Saar co-founder Ananya Singhal, this location had a significant impact on the project.

"The Strand is right next to Somerset House and right next to India House," Singhal told Dezeen.

"Somerset House is where the British Navy was administered from during the colonial period, and India House is where the Indian High Commission is," he continued. "So this site has a very interesting history behind the relationship between India and the UK."

The Pangolin Shield pavilion also faces a bust of India's first prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru.

To Singhal, placing the pavilion in this location was an opportunity to underline the new relationship that India has with the UK "and possibly the world", he said.

"We're an Indo-UK practice working with a British engineer, so there was something about this project and the site which kind of brought that combination together," Singhal said.

The Pangolin Shield was designed by Studio Saar and structural engineers Atelier One, led by founder Neil Thomas. It was constructed using a bamboo grid shell, which the studios wanted to use because of the material's many positive characteristics.

"It's lightweight, it's durable, it grows very quickly; once you finish with it, it's biodegradable, and you can make super interesting shapes from it," Singhal said.

The gridded shell structure that forms the base – and which is strengthened by steel fastenings – was then covered in two very different types of shields.

On top of the bamboo grid is a first layer, made from traditional Indian police shields constructed out of lathis, a type of bamboo stick.

This first layer is then covered by knups, woven rain shields that are traditionally used by farmers in the north-east of India.

Read:

Studio Saar creates forest-like pavilion at Design Mumbai

"The police shields were designed by the British colonial rulers to keep riots down in India all those years ago; it's really beautiful, the idea of making it a part of the structure that shelters both visitors and the locals here," Singhal said.

"The knups are from Meghalaya, the wettest place on Earth – it gets more than two metres of rain per year and its name literally means 'the land of the clouds'," he continued.

The design of the pavilion, which resembles a creature covered in scales, was also inspired by Singhal's work outside of Studio Saar.

"I'm a wildlife photographer and conservationist, and one of the animals that I hear about a lot is the pangolin, which is the most trafficked mammal on Earth," he explained. "So I wanted to create a structure that brought the pangolin into conversation."

Inside the pavilion, visitors can admire a sculpture of the pangolin and look at the drawings for the project.

As the pavilion was damaged when it was transported from India to the UK, it will be shown with an interior scaffold during London Design Festival (LDF) due to "abundant caution," Singhal said.

"It's a public space and there are going to be drunk people coming up and down this street", he said in reference to the risk of the pavilion being damaged.

Overall, Singhal believes that the project is a good representation of the values that Studio Saar stands for.

"Something which we really hold dear as a practice is the idea you can take small, humble, crafted things and combine them to make amazing things," he said.

"And that's the piece that we've practised in many areas, and what we would really love to do, and that's what we're doing here with the police shields and the knups."

Other projects on show at London Design Festival include Craft x Tech, which explores Japanese craft in a contemporary way, and Lozi's modular plywood furniture.

The photography is by Taran Wilkhu.

The Pangolin Shield is on show at The Strand, WC2 1HL, from 12 to 20 September. See our London Design Festival 2026 guide on Dezeen Events Guide for information about the many other exhibitions, installations and talks that take place during the week.

item.content:encoded:
Tiles decorated with hair and a dissolving washbasin made of soap are among the student projects featured in Behind Closed Doors, an exhibition by the Design Academy Eindhoven and Kaldewei at Berlin design festival Currents.

The exhibition featured standout projects born from a 10-week educational partnership between the bathroom brand and students of the academy's Social Design master's degree that explored the future of the bathroom.

As part of the collaboration, the students were asked to investigate how bathrooms can be reimagined in a more circular way that doesn't just conserve resources but also encourages more circular behaviours and habits in its users.

"We gave them the idea that in a circular world, Kaldewei would not produce a new bathtub anymore because we would reuse our old bathtubs, give them a new surface and build them in again," the company's head of design Christian Büttner told Dezeen.

"So what the students really explored for us was: what are the barriers against this that we have in our head?"

Among the eight featured projects, some of the most visceral explored how we can overcome the natural aversion we have against waste materials – especially ones that have passed through the hands of other people.

Design Academy students Sarah Kinzer and Moss A Moschen visited student bathrooms on their street in Eindhoven and documented the traces of use that were left behind – black mould, clumps of hair, limescale on a showerhead.

The duo abstracted these patterns in a collection of steel tiles, some even incorporating real strands of their own hair, to find beauty rather than revulsion in the intimate history of these materials.

"We try to make an aesthetic of disgust," Moschen explained. "If we want to talk about circularity, but as a society we hold expectations towards very clean and polished materials, how can we even do that?"

"So I think we just tried to flip the narrative and question what happens when something that we call disgusting is intentionally part of the design language."

In a similar vein, Carlotta Talkenberger felted a bath mat from human hair to explore the double standard inherent in using animal hair to make many of the products around us while shunning our own.

And in Ian Chu's project Wash Away Your Guilt, discarded cooking oil is turned into soap and used to form a washbasin that slowly dissolves with every use, exploring both the practical and moral implications of circularity.

"She was also questioning a little bit if circularity is a concept that we hide behind so we don't feel guilty," Moschen explained.

Read:

"Industry in Germany is no longer open to what design can do" say Currents Berlin organisers

As Europe's record-breaking heatwaves reduced the continent's water supplies to historic lows, other students shared speculative projects about how limited access to this crucial resource could reshape our habits and spaces.

A satirical film by Hanxiao Xu depicts a community that reuses its bathwater and attributes it with mythical healing properties, while Philipp Hohnerlein and Gabriela Augustyniak imagine that bathing will cease entirely.

Instead, their Bathtube project (top image) suggests tapping into the waste heat of data centres and turning their pipes into impromptu hammams, offering the warmth and comfort of a bath without the water wastage.

Nature's resources also take centre stage in a project from Guadalupe Vanini Cervini that explores the indigenous principle of the Honourable Harvest – a "covenant of reciprocity" stipulating how to responsibly take from nature and give back in return.

In this spirit, she used naturally fallen reeds from the wetlands around Eindhoven to create a series of sculptures set within that same landscape, but transported to Berlin for the sake of the exhibition.

Another exploration of more-than-human design came from Tina Lehnhardt, who created a performance around a series of costumes – embodying black mould, moisture, a dead skin cell and a humidity-loving insect known as a silverfish – to humanise the other life forms with which we share our bathrooms.

Finally, taking a more playful take on the topic, Xinliang Zhou created a simple method and instructions for how to turn everyday bathroom items into musical instruments and every shower into a jam session.

The Behind Closed Doors exhibition formed part of the inaugural Currents design festival in Berlin, which the founders argue is well on its way to establishing itself as Germany's new design capital.

Currents 2026 took place from 10 to 12 September 2026 at various locations across Berlin, Germany. For other design events around the world, visit Dezeen Events Guide.

The Vipp453 Swivel chair is defined by its architectural silhouette, created by an aluminium frame that wraps fluidly from the arms around the padded backrest.

The backrest is substantial enough to provide comfort and support over long periods of sitting, while also giving the chair a light, airy appearance thanks to its suspended design.

Part of a line of similar chairs from Vipp, a family-owned company founded in 1939, the Vipp453 Swivel chair adds a four-star base with either castors or gliders and a 360-degree rotation.

Vipp imagines it working well in offices and conference rooms where an elevated aesthetic is desired, as well as in home offices where a bulky task chair would be unwelcome.

The chair is available upholstered in either black, camel or green leather or Dark Sand textile — finishes that continue the refined, mid-century look.

item.content:encoded:
Look-but-don't-touch design exhibitions are inherently unfulfilling so it's good that some designers are finding ways to let people properly interact with their work, writes Alice Fisher.

In the 1990s as a student in London, I got a summer job at a famous department store. I was a sales assistant for towels and robes working next to the bathroom furniture department which, true to the shop's reputation for ostentatious luxury, included some incredibly ornate toilets.

One morning, word spread around the staff that someone had – somehow – managed to use a display toilet for its intended purpose. Reactions ranged from outraged disgust to amused respect.

I so often want to climb into the displays of beautiful furniture I'm looking at and settle in

Personally, I was envious – imagine clambering into that sterile room set and settling on the porcelain throne. Even the most prestigious customer wouldn't get away with that.

I'm surprised how often I think about that toilet when visiting design exhibitions these days. Not for any weird reason – the only stool I like to see is one that's handmade, preferably from reclaimed wood – but because I so often want to climb into the displays of beautiful furniture I'm looking at and settle in.

Sadly, at most design festivals that would be as shocking and frowned upon as hopping onto the lav in a department store display.

Read:

Five galleries injecting renewed energy into the London design scene

Looking but not touching or interacting with design is, to my mind, a strange and impotent experience. I spend so much time staring really intently at chairs trying to imagine what they feel like, when what I really want to do is loll in them.

The two things I overuse the most at London Design Festival (LDF) and other such events are my camera phone – obvs – and the surreptitious finger. You know what I mean – the index finger you slide out at hip height to feel the buttery softness of a leather chair arm, or the cool surprise of a marble tabletop, when the publicist and designer are looking the other way.

Just to be clear, I'm not stupid. I understand the financial and creative investment that studios and designers have put into these displays. I know that most of the furniture on show is a prototype or produced at great personal cost to the maker and that letting the clumsy, feckless public loose on these masterpieces is not a good idea.

Many design-week visitors want to experience furniture in a natural way

And yet… wouldn't it be great if there was an idiot-proof version of the furniture you could have a go on?

Cast your mind back over the most discussed or fondly remembered exhibits at recent design weeks and you can see I'm not the only person who feels this way. Paul Cocksedge, Alison Brooks and Waugh Thistleton all made landmark wooden LDF installations in recent years that could be sat on, walked through or even climbed up.

I'm so pleased that the AHEC exhibition Wood for the Trees, which debuted at Copenhagen's 3 Days of Design (3DD) in June, will also appear at LDF this week. The show includes beautiful rocking wooden benches by Benchmark, which are such a great place to sit.

Read:

Read LDF edition of Dezeen Dispatch online now!

Also at 3DD this year was an outsized conversation pit. This version of the 1950s favourite – in beautiful lemon linen – was a collaboration between furniture brand Vipp and Spanish architecture studio Mesura. Big enough to hold 60 people, visitors were encouraged to slip off their shoes and climb inside using swimming pool-style ladders. Most design critics opted to bounce like toddlers at soft play rather than hold a meaningful conversation, which made the experience even more delightful.

Metamorphosis in Motion by architect Lina Ghotmeh at this year's Milan design week gave a similar thrill. Watching people explore Ghotmeh's magenta maze, which filled the courtyard at the Palazzo Litta, was a pleasure.

The trend for staging shows in apartments rather than sterile showrooms also reflects how many design-week visitors want to experience furniture in a natural way. While design shop Artemest is probably the OG brand for turning fabulous apartments into even-more-fabulous fantasy exhibition spaces during Milan, I think French vintage dealer Antoine Billore's Loreto apartment for perfume house L'Artisan Parfumeur this year was the one in which I really wanted to sit down and pretend it was mine.

"I'd be filmed by a load of strangers while making coffee in the morning," she said. "It was pretty extreme."

British designer Charlotte Taylor's breakout show was Home from Home at 3DD 2025 (pictured). She not only curated this exhibition of work by 40 furniture designers held in an apartment at Noura Residency on Sankt Peders Stræde, but also lived in the space during the design festival.

Recently, Taylor told me that, although the idea was to get away from the "untouchable tableau" of the typical design show, she hadn't expected visitors to get quite so comfortable, quite so quickly in her personal space. "It became a performative piece, to the extent that I'd be filmed by a load of strangers while making coffee in the morning," she said. "It was pretty extreme."

She should have held a lottery that gave visitors the opportunity to apply to spend the night there themselves. I can think of few things that design fans would like more.

All I would like designers to do is think of any way it's possible for visitors to engage with their beautiful creations beyond the look-but-don't-touch of a standard design fair. Using a toilet absolutely crosses the line, but is sitting down, or even touching, really asking too much?

Alice Fisher is a lifestyle journalist based in London. She was previously lifestyle editor at The Observer, and has also written for The Guardian and the Financial Times, among others.

item.content:encoded:
With London Design Festival underway, we asked long-standing mayor of London Sadiq Khan for his thoughts on the festival and what to see this year.

Amy Peacock: Why do you believe London's design scene is worth investing in, and what role does London Design Festival play in this?

Sadiq Khan: London has a remarkable history of producing designs that have become global icons. Visionaries such as Thomas Heatherwick and Norman Foster have reimagined architecture and public spaces, while Vivienne Westwood revolutionised fashion with her rebellious designs, and celebrated product designer Tom Dixon and multidisciplinary artist Es Devlin are all showing why London's design is an international success story.

I'm delighted that LDF plays a key role in the success of the industry, showcasing, celebrating and developing our leading talent. The festival is an incredible advert, drawing international attention, investment and visitors as it welcomes more than 600,000 visitors.

I'm hugely proud to support the festival and over the past 10 years have invested £2.2 million that has helped to unlock £1.23 billion for the economy through jobs and investment.

Amy Peacock: What are you looking forward to seeing this year at LDF?

Sadiq Khan: London Design Festival is a huge highlight in the capital's cultural calendar because there are so many great events taking place. There's a lot to look forward to, including The Pangolin Shield, which will be a significant installation on the Strand.

There are design districts that showcase 11 neighbourhoods across the city as local studios, showrooms, galleries and cultural venues open their doors with exhibitions, installations, events and talks, while the V&A continues its long-standing relationship with the festival with Awakenings.

Amy Peacock: How does London's design scene compare to other cities? Do you think it's possible for LDF to have an impact on the scale of design festivals in Milan and Copenhagen, and how does the UK no longer being in the EU have an impact on this?

Sadiq Khan: Our capital is a powerhouse for the creative industries and LDF is a fantastic example of our influence in the design industry. The festival promotes our city's creativity, drawing in the country's greatest thinkers, practitioners, retailers and educators to deliver an unmissable celebration of design. That's why it is one of the world's leading design events and has served as the blueprint for design weeks and festivals globally.

However, there is no doubt that the UK's departure from the EU has made it harder for London's design industry to trade, collaborate and recruit talent across Europe. Increased paperwork, barriers for the movement of creative talent and reduced access to EU funding have brought challenges, but despite all this, London continues to be a thriving and welcoming place for designers.

item.content:encoded:
Designers Bahbak Hashemi-Nezhad and Rafael El Baz have used traditional biscuit moulds to create Sweet Terrain, a collection of wall tiles for a HS2 station made from clay excavated during its construction.

Hashemi-Nezhad and El Baz salvaged 12 tonnes of clay dug up from the site of Old Oak Common, a station under construction in London designed by WilkinsonEyre for the high-speed rail network HS2, to make the playful collection.

The tiles have distinctive reliefs made with moulds modelled on wooden tools traditionally used to create Ma'amoul – cookies originating in the Arab world. The design draws on the designers' visits to patisseries in west London belonging to Middle Eastern bakers who migrated from Lebanon and Syria.

It is hoped to shine a light on their stories and help bring place-based identity and connections to local communities into the vast and controversial HS2 project.

"The goals were to make hyper-local objects that resonate with those who would ultimately see and use them, and in doing so instil a sense of pride and embed narrative that isn't possible with off-the-shelf products," Hashemi-Nezhad told Dezeen.

"Beyond the resourcefulness and circularity of the project, we wanted to create something meaningful, literally from the bottom up, by engaging local communities and embedding the work for the generations that follow them," added El Baz.

"Infrastructure projects, however large or small, can be humanised and made culturally resonant through design."

According to the designers, the Sweet Terrain tiles are set to be used in the station's "quiet spaces", such as multi-faith zones, toilets and corridors.

The exact number of tiles that will be used is yet to be confirmed, but Hashemi-Nezhad said the number will be in the thousands.

Sweet Terrain's initial design process began by diverting 12 tonnes of construction soil from landfill. It was then smoothed and refined, forming the ideal consistency for tile making.

Production was carried out with Craven Dunnill Jackfield – one of Britain's oldest and last remaining traditional tilemakers, which has previously created tiles for London Underground.

Read:

London Underground waste repurposed into tiles for tube stations

Together with Craven Dunnill Jackfield, the duo developed 3D scans of the biscuit moulds to form the tiles, which have been made in various sizes and depths to ensure optimal style for installation in the public realm.

"Too shallow and it loses its tactility; too proud and it risks chipping and damage due to vandalism," said Hashemi-Nezhad.

Now the designers are working with the manufacturer's glaze lab to experiment with different colour and texture finishes.

However, they are set on using hand-dipped glazes, which they believe will help add a "human touch" to the wider infrastructure project.

The bakers with whom Hashemi-Nezhad and El Baz have consulted on the project have described the work as "an act of recognition".

"When these tiles enter the public realm in the new station, it will bring so much joy and pride to us bakers, as well as our communities and families," baker Vasken Jermakian of Sweetland Bakery said.

The HS2 network has been highly controversial, for reasons including its environmental impact on the Chilterns – an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty (AONB) through which it cuts.

Dezeen recently published construction photos of Old Oak Common station, for which the tiles are being made. Once complete, it will be one of the largest transport interchanges in the UK.

Designer Hashemi-Nezhad is currently a designer in residence at CCA Tashkent, which recently opened its hub within a "basilica-like" tram depot overhauled by Studio KO in the Uzbekistan capital.

item.content:encoded:
White lime-rendered walls frame Casa Amona, a two-storey home and studio in Mexico, designed by local architecture studio Colar to support multi-generational living.

Perched beside a wooded hillside in San Cristóbal de las Casas, the 155-square-metre residence contains a one-bedroom house that can be adapted into a two-bed, alongside a studio and a guest bedroom.

Colar designed its angular form to prioritise views of the surrounding hillside in several directions, allowing each room to forge "a different relationship to the landscape".

This is enabled by a series of sheltered terraces that punctuate the home's upper floor, along with a combination of slim and large windows that characterise the home's exterior.

"The house is conceived as a continuous dialogue between domestic life and the landscape, with the garden becoming an active part of the spatial experience," Colar told Dezeen.

"Rather than relying on a single dominant view, the project uses different openings, orientations, and types of windows to create a series of distinct relationships with the garden and the surrounding landscape."

At the home's front, a sheltered entryway provides access to the main dwelling, while a separate entrance leads into the studio space, which sits beneath a wooden roof and is flanked by a spacious planted courtyard.

Inside, the home features a stacked layout of rooms designed to function as independent units. This includes living spaces on the ground floor and a bedroom above.

To accommodate multi-generational living, an enclosed ground-floor living space can be converted into a bedroom without architectural intervention.

Upstairs, the main bedroom space is accompanied by a small study and complemented by three terraces overlooking the landscape.

Read:

Colar revives adobe structure to create pared-back home in Mexico

"The house is organised as a series of spatially autonomous but interconnected units, allowing different forms of occupation over time," the studio said.

"The adjacent workshop, with its independent access, provides a space for artistic work and family gatherings while also allowing for autonomous living when needed."

Informed by local building techniques, the home's lime-rendered concrete blockwork and brick walls are left exposed across the interior and exterior, paired with carpentry and clay tile floors.

"The material palette draws from local building traditions while allowing their constructional logic to be expressed in a contemporary way," the studio explained.

Also in Mexico, the studio recently updated and extended a dilapidated adobe structure to create a single-storey home in Chiapas, and Studio Font perched a cliffside home in Mazunte atop a series of inhabitable concrete columns.
